heading: Desktop app guide
text: This guide covers the fim desktop app ( fim-gui ). It assumes you know the finite island model and differentiation statistics. It records what this implementation does, which conventions it uses, and where each control lives. For the model itself, start with the introduction to the finite island model . In the app, open this guide with Help in the left rail or Help > Desktop help . Press F1 for help on the focused field or the current screen.

heading: Before you compare with the literature
text: Read implementation conventions before you compare a result with a published value. Four conventions most often explain an apparent disagreement: N counts individuals per deme; the engine uses gene copies. The scalar m is the fraction of a deme's parents drawn from the other demes, not a redraw from all d demes. A generation is migrate, then drift, then mutate. Generation 0 is a Dirichlet prior (or explicit p 0 ), not a sampled population.

heading: Open documents
text: The tab bar below the title lists open configurations, runs, and studies. Each tab keeps its own screen and history. Switching tabs does not stop work in another tab. Opening a result that is already open selects its existing tab. A new configuration always starts as a separate draft. Open tabs are held in memory for this window; they are not restored after a restart. Saved results are unaffected. Close a tab with its × , File > Close tab , or Delete while the tab has focus. A configuration with unsaved changes asks whether to save, discard, or keep it. An active run, saved run, or sweep offers the appropriate pause or stop action. Closing a tab never deletes saved results. Right-click a tab for Close other tabs and Close all results . Close all results closes completed run and sweep-result tabs, not configurations or saved runs. Unsaved or active tabs use the usual close dialog one at a time: Keep skips that tab; Escape cancels the rest of the bulk close. With more than 12 tabs open, a notice offers Close all results . This is a reminder, not a limit.

heading: Implementation conventions
text: This page lists the conventions that most often matter when you compare a fim result with a published formula or another simulator. Each item links to the authoritative reference. The desktop app and the command line follow the same conventions.

heading: Population size and ploidy
text: The N (individuals/deme) field and the YAML key N count individuals . The engine uses gene copies per deme and locus, where c is the ploidy (haploid 1 through tetraploid 4). The conversion happens once, when the configuration is read. Every statistic, closed-form prediction, and derived timescale uses gene copies. Explore and sweeps also take N in individuals and apply the form's ploidy. N: 225 with ploidy: diploid and N: 450 with ploidy: haploid are the same genetic process. They are recorded as different population descriptions and receive different run IDs. Per-deme sizes are supported. Every operator and size-weighted option uses each deme's gene-copy count. See N , ploidy , and population unit .

heading: Migration
text: A scalar m is the fraction of a deme's parental pool drawn from the other demes. That incoming fraction is size-weighted across the other demes; with equal sizes each contributes . Some papers instead redraw a fraction from all d demes, including home. Convert with . For , equals a redraw rate of . A full matrix row k gives destination k 's source weights. Rows must sum to 1. Matrix weights are authoritative and are not rescaled by deme size. A named topology's rate is each deme's total outgoing fraction, split evenly among its neighbors. Do not apply the island-model conversion above to a topology. migrant sampling continuous (the default) mixes frequencies deterministically. stochastic draws migrant gene-copy counts each generation; the mean is unchanged, and N sets the variance. See m , migrant_sampling , and migration source .

heading: Generation order
text: One generation is migrate → drift → mutate : migration changes parental frequencies, drift draws whole gene copies, and each new copy mutates independently with probability μ. Papers that write drift → migrate → mutate can describe the same process when the state is translated at the generation boundary; do not add a one-generation lag. See operator order and the generation pipeline .

heading: Generation 0 and founding
text: Generation 0 is the initial conditions draw: a continuous Dirichlet prior, an equilibrium split, an explicit p 0 , or fixed alleles per deme. A Dirichlet or explicit p 0 need not lie on the lattice. Treat a generation-0 statistic as a property of the prior, not of a sampled population. Generation 1 is the first generation on the lattice. Generation 0 is never included in a convergence average. Equilibrium split simulates an ancestral population first and splits it. Its window, tolerance, and cap are separate from the main run's. See initial conditions .

heading: Mutation
text: μ is a per-gene-copy probability per generation, applied after drift. Derive from μb sets each locus's μ from a per-base rate and the locus length. Edit μb, not the derived per-locus μ. infinite_alleles (the default) gives every mutation a new, globally unique allele ID. finite_alleles bounds a locus to states for length ; mutations can recur to existing states. Founding alleles use locus-relative IDs. See mu , deriving mu from a per-base rate , and mutation model .

heading: Statistics
text: Reported statistics are functions of the population frequencies, not finite-sample estimators. No sample-size correction is applied. Pooled frequencies use equal deme weights except where deme weighting applies. That setting affects only E ST , ( Delta ), and I ( MI ). Across loci, D and G ST default to a ratio of mean heterozygosities ( locus_aggregation: ratio_of_means ). A mean of per-locus ratios is a different estimand. For time averages, expected value chooses between the mean of a statistic's values and the statistic of the mean heterozygosities. Every report carries both. An undefined value is not evidence of zero differentiation. The app shows mathematical symbols ( H ST , , I ). Configuration fields, saved files, and exports keep literal keys ( H_ST , Delta , MI ). See notation and aggregation , deme_weighting , locus_aggregation , and convergence_estimate .

heading: When a run stops
text: A run first discards a burn-in , then averages each watched statistic over an evidence window. It stops when each average's standard error meets precision at the chosen confidence , and the effective sample size reaches its floor. convergence burn-in and max generations default to auto , derived from the slowest locus's relaxation time. The derived values appear beside Run simulation before you start. With several watched statistics, all (the default) waits for every one. any stops at the first, so the others may not be converged. Reaching max generations is a valid, non-converged result. The report gives the precision achieved. A short run is not evidence of equilibrium. See convergence and the quick reference .

heading: Batches and replicates
text: n_replicates defaults to 200 , not 1. Set it to 1 for a single run; there is no separate batch-mode control. Replicate i uses child i of numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed) . With stop the batch early on (the default), a batch stops when every watched statistic's across-replicate Student's- t interval has half-width at most precision , after at least replicate minimum replicates. n_replicates remains a hard cap. Replicates are considered in replicate order on every engine, not in completion order. Batch intervals describe uncertainty across independent replicates. The app labels them "uncertainty across N independent replicates". See n_replicates , stop_batch_early , and batches .

heading: Engines and seeds
text: execution engine changes speed, not results. lineal (the reference), generational , and generational-vector produce the same trajectory, bit for bit, for the same seed on the same machine. auto chooses one from the deme count and locus capacity. Across machines, the compiled engines are reproducible statistically, not necessarily bit for bit. max workers affects only elapsed time. max concurrent replicates is recorded and can change adaptive-batch results. Run IDs are hashes of the configuration. Names and descriptions are not part of the ID. See engine_backend and reproduce a run .

heading: Configure
text: Configure edits one configuration: the model, its structure, the stopping rule, and an optional sweep. Each field shows a short tooltip on hover or keyboard focus. Press F1 in a field to open its entry in the configuration reference .

text: Run settings… opens Run settings for this configuration : the Settings dialog's execution, convergence, Expert, and storage controls, scoped to this configuration only: Control YAML key execution engine engine_backend n_replicates n_replicates max generations max_generations confidence confidence convergence burn-in convergence_burn_in precision precision expected value convergence_estimate precision method precision_method replicate averaging window replicate_averaging_window max concurrent replicates max_concurrent_replicates JIT jit auto-vector min d, auto-vector max capacity auto_vector_min_d , auto_vector_max_capacity trajectory retention, trajectory stride, thinning start trajectory retention keys Defaults come from Settings . Apply to this run validates the values against the current model and applies them without changing saved Settings. For example, max_generations: auto cannot be derived when both migration and mutation are zero; the editor reports the error and leaves the configuration unchanged. max workers is a property of this computer, not of the run. heading: Loaded run settings
text: A configuration you load can supply its own run settings. This applies to Examples… ( Load into Configure and Run it ), File > Load example… , Load configuration… , and Clone on Home. The loaded values apply to this run only ; your Settings are not changed. A run setting omitted from the file takes the simulator default, as fim run would. When any loaded value differs from your Settings, a notice on Configure and on the run view lists each difference side by side: Make these my Settings saves the loaded values as your Settings. Max workers is not changed. Edit this run… opens the run settings editor. Use saved Settings fills it from your Settings; Restore loaded settings restores the loaded values. Neither applies until you choose Apply to this run . Dismiss hides the notice; the run still uses the loaded values. The run settings item in the parameter strip remains while values differ; select it to show the notice again. If you change Settings later, the notice compares against the new Settings. To adopt your Settings for this run, choose Run settings… , then Use saved Settings , then Apply to this run . That copies a snapshot; later changes to Settings do not alter it. File > New

heading: Load, save, and examples
text: Load configuration… and Save configuration… read and write YAML in the same format as fim run . Examples… opens the bundled worked examples. View YAML shows the configuration; Load into Configure gives an editable copy; Open saved result opens the finished result without computing. See examples . File > Load example… opens the preset picker, which also lists presets you saved with Save current as… .

heading: Naming the next run
text: Run name and Run description label the next run, then clear when it starts. They are hidden while Sweep is ticked, because a sweep names its own runs. The study selector at the bottom chooses where the run is filed. It starts at Default study . New study… creates a study with a name and an optional description. Names and descriptions are stored in metadata.json and are never part of the run ID. See names and documentation .

heading: Run, sweep, and explore
text: Run starts the configuration. With n_replicates above 1, the run is a batch. Before you start, the run view shows the derived burn-in and cap beside Run simulation . Check them against the model's timescale. If a completed result already exists for the same configuration and software version, the app reuses it instead of computing again. Tick Sweep and choose Set up sweep… to vary parameters. Run then executes the sweep in the chosen study. See sweeps . Explore opens closed-form predictions for the current N, d, m, and μ. See Explore .

heading: Validation
text: Invalid input is reported when you run. The app returns to Configure and marks the field. Unknown or misspelled YAML keys are rejected, never ignored. A configuration that is incomplete or invalid can still be kept with Save for later ; it is saved as a Draft.

heading: Run and results
text: The run view shows one configuration's run in three states: initial, running, and completed. Run and Results in the rail both open it. A single run ( n_replicates: 1 ) and a batch share the view; the batch view adds replicate summaries.

heading: Before a run
text: The initial state shows the founding state (generation 0) and the derived convergence schedule beside Run simulation , for example: Convergence: burn-in 104,338 generations, cap 399,728 (derived; this model needs about 19,693 generations to forget its starting state) Check the burn-in and cap against the model's timescale before you start. See why a run takes so long . Run simulation always starts from the current configuration, even when a previous result is displayed. Edit configuration returns to Configure.

heading: While a run executes
text: Allele frequencies, statistic trajectories, and progress update live. Batch scatter plots pool the replicates in progress. Deme selectors (initially deme 1 against deme 2) apply to subsequent updates of the scatter plot and pairwise statistics. Cancel stops the run. Cancellation or an error keeps the last rendered view and adds a status banner. Pause appears while a saved run executes; it stops at a checkpoint. The run continues if you switch tabs or screens.

heading: Graphs
text: Graphs selects which graphs are visible. Settings controls how many sit side by side and the scatter-plot point style. Graph Shows Allele frequencies by deme pair Each allele's frequency in one deme against another; axes span 0–1 Statistic trajectories Each shown statistic against generation, with references Allele composition by deme Stacked allele composition of each deme Allele-frequency spectrum Empirical frequency spectrum, with an optional Wright beta overlay Isolation-by-distance identity decay Pairwise identity against migration-graph distance The last three are drawn for completed results; batches pool them across replicates. Double-click a graph to open it in a larger frame with the scrubber and statistics table. The frame offers zoom ( − , + ), Fit , Reset view , and Export image… . Escape or Close returns it to the run view.

heading: Statistic trajectories
text: References. Single runs draw the analytic equilibrium line and, where available, the expected trajectory for D , G ST , H S , H T , and H ST . Expected trajectories start from the seeded founding state and support unequal deme sizes and explicit migration matrices up to 24 demes. They are omitted for per-locus mutation rates, equilibrium-split founding, and larger matrices. They are model expectations, not stochastic paths; with few loci, the mean of a ratio can differ from the ratio of expectations. See convergence_estimate . f₀ (identity recovery) overlays Whitlock's (1992) closed-form identity-by-descent recovery after a founder event, computed from this configuration's N and m alone. It is a reference, not a measurement of this run. It is off by default and hidden when N or m is not a plain scalar. See identity recovery . Show selects Every generation , Trailing mean , or Cumulative mean . Band selects ±1 or ±2 (the default) standard errors for means. With Every generation , the band shows standard deviations over the evidence window instead. Reference curves are averaged over the same windows. Cumulative averaging begins at the recorded averaging start, or after one convergenc

heading: Statistics table and hover readouts
text: The statistics table is also the trajectory legend: select a row to show or hide its line. Select an underlined statistic name to open its reference entry . Choose… in the table caption opens Statistics shown in Settings, which chooses the rows; hidden statistics are still in the saved report. Hover a row for its window mean, standard error, generation range, and standardized difference from the window-averaged prediction: mean 0.5506 ± 0.0048 over generations 1,399–174,966 (173,568 generations; 1 SE); predicted 0.5448, +1.2 SE At the final generation, the window is the monitor's stopping window. It can be longer than the configured convergence window, because the monitor widens it to assess precision. "Not yet noise-adequate" marks a mean that has not met the precision requirement. The first-order autoregressive standard error used here accounts for correlation between neighboring generations. It can underestimate uncertainty when relaxation has several time scales. The stopping rule itself uses Geyer's initial positive sequence; see how precise is the reported value? The row also shows (observed minus predicted at the selected generation) and the trajectory mean squared error, fo

heading: Completed single runs
text: The report shows each statistic, the stop outcome (converged or reached the cap), and the precision achieved. With more than one retained generation, the scrubber plays back or scrubs through the saved trajectory. Thinned runs scrub only retained generations. Deme selectors update the scatter plot and pairwise statistics at the scrubbed generation. Pairs not saved in pairwise.json are recomputed from the trajectory on demand.

heading: Completed batches
text: The scatter plot pools the final states of all replicates. A table lists each replicate's status, final generation, and statistics. Open on a replicate shows it as a single run. Intervals are labeled "uncertainty across N independent replicates". They are Student's- t intervals over replicate window means; see the across-replicate interval . A batch can stop before n_replicates when stop the batch early is on; the number of replicates shown is the number that ran.

heading: Pause, save for later, and resume
text: Save for later keeps the configuration as a saved run under Saved runs on Home. An incomplete or invalid configuration is saved as a Draft. Run simulation creates and starts a saved run. After Pause , Run simulation in the same tab resumes it from its checkpoint. A resumed run reproduces an uninterrupted run. The desktop app runs one saved run at a time. See saved runs in the desktop app for every state and action.

heading: Files
text: Open output folder (or File > Reveal output folder ) shows the run's files: manifest.json , report.json , trajectory.tlog , pairwise.json , and, for a batch, summary.json plus one replicate-NNN/ folder per replicate. See output schemas .

heading: Explore
text: Explore evaluates closed-form predictions from N, d, m, and μ without running a simulation. Use it to locate a regime, check a timescale, or choose sweep points before you spend computation.

heading: Inputs and units
text: N (individuals/deme) is in individuals. Explore applies the ploidy of the current configuration to obtain gene copies. d (demes) , m (migration rate) , and μ (mutation rate) use the scalar island-model conventions; see migration . A field commits when you leave it or press Enter. Predictions then update. Explore never changes Configure until you choose Run this for real or Sweep this for real .

heading: Predictions
text: The table groups predictions under Statistics , Equilibrium diversity , and Identity and regime . It covers differentiation measures, diversity, entropy, effective allele counts, identity-recovery timescales, and whether mutation is negligible. Definitions are in the statistics reference , including identity recovery and mutation-negligible equilibrium . Predictions that do not depend on a parameter are flat along it. For example, analytic D is independent of N, and identity-recovery metrics are independent of μ.

heading: Curves and surfaces
text: View selects Curve: one parameter or Surface: two parameters . A surface uses Rows and Columns as its two axes. Select a statistic row to chart it over the chosen parameter range. Charts group compatible units (proportions, nats, allele counts, generations). The slider evaluates predictions along the range without changing the input fields.

heading: From prediction to simulation
text: Run this for real copies the four inputs to Configure, selects a new Study, and starts from your Settings. Choose a sweep… picks sweep points for the displayed parameters: an interval, a count, and a spacing. The spacing is the axis scale (linear or log) or even steps of a predicted response chosen in Place points by the response of ( D , G ST , E ST , H S , or H T ). Response spacing crowds points where the prediction changes fastest, such as the migration threshold. The exact points and the planned sweep size are shown. Removing a point switches to an explicit list. Sweep this for real copies the inputs to Configure, ticks Sweep , and stores the axes. See sweeps . Response spacing produces an explicit list of values, so the sweep stays reproducible without the closed form.

heading: Limits
text: Predictions assume equilibrium and the scalar finite island model. They do not represent topologies, matrices, unequal sizes, stochastic migrant sampling, or finite alleles. Typical-deme entropy is approximate, especially at . Explore makes no claim about how long a run takes to reach the prediction. Use the derived burn-in shown before a run, and see convergence . For programmatic access, see the Python statistics API .

heading: Sweeps
text: A sweep runs one configuration over a set of parameter values. Every point is an ordinary run, filed in one Study. The desktop app and fim sweep share the same specification, storage, and results; the command-line equivalent of each action is given in parentheses. Full semantics are in sweep a parameter .

heading: Set up a sweep
text: In Configure, tick Sweep and choose Set up sweep… . Under What varies , choose a parameter and its values for each axis. Add axis adds another; there is no limit. Common parameters are listed first; every other sweepable setting is under More parameters . List- and group-valued settings ( p_0 , mu_b , loci , expert ) and seed cannot be swept. Combine the axes : Every combination (a grid) , with the first axis changing slowest, or Together, value by value (equal counts) ( strategy: zip ). Check the live point count. Show every point lists them with their validity; an incompatible combination, such as a torus whose rows × columns differs from d, is listed with its reason ( fim sweep plan ). Choose Done , then Run . The sweep runs in the Study selected at the bottom of Configure. A Study holds at most one sweep. N on a sweep axis counts individuals per deme, as everywhere else. A Nm axis sets with N in individuals and replaces m . Explore's Sweep this for real fills the same setup; see Explore .

heading: Recording and disk
text: Keep chooses what each point stores: Choice YAML retention Stores Everything full Every generation Every Nth generation thinned One generation in every stride after a start Recent generations, thinning further back tapered The most recent generations in full, thinning further back; frames grow with the logarithm of run length Statistics only statistics No trajectory log; report, summary, scatter plot, and a decimated history of at most 2,048 generations For tapered , Recent generations kept in full sets keep_last , and Keep the burn-in frames too keeps the transient. Statistic history is Compact (the sweep default: values rounded to about a hundredth of the precision, which changes no reported answer) or Exact . The dialog shows Time , Disk , and what was Measured for the points still to run. Ranges reflect unknown convergence times. The time estimate comes from a brief probe of this computer's engine ("Measuring the engine…"); results are cached in sweep-throughput.json beside your preferences. A point whose existing run kept less than the sweep requests is recomputed; a run that kept more is reused.

heading: Seeds and reuse
text: Seeds : Independent points (recommended) gives point i the seed base seed + i × n_replicates , so no two points share a replicate seed. The same seed at every point ( seed_policy: same ) uses the base seed throughout. A point's run ID is a hash of its configuration. A sweep that overlaps an earlier one reuses identical points, including seed, made by the same software version. Points at once sets concurrency; Automatic fills the cores. Results do not depend on it.

heading: Progress
text: The progress view shows each point's state, the time remaining, and each finished point's duration. Points with the longest estimated duration start first; scheduling never changes a point's configuration or result. A failed point is recorded and the sweep continues. A point that fails for a transient reason is retried once. Cancel sweep stops the sweep and pauses the points in flight; finished points stay in the Study. A sweep locks its Study while it runs. Another process that tries to run the same Study stops with a message instead.

heading: Results
text: View results opens the results card. View selects: Final values: the chosen Statistic Across one axis. To compare values of a second axis, set and to "(none: a line)" and choose Curves by . Each value gets a color, marker shape, error bars, and an optional theory curve. Two axes can also be drawn as a heat map, whose Show menu offers Simulation , Theory , Simulation minus theory , and the difference as a fraction of theory. How each point got there: the statistic against generation, one curve per Curves by value. The band is the interval of the mean over replicates still running; a dotted line marks the end of burn-in; a dashed stretch marks where fewer than half the replicates are still running; a hollow end marker marks a point whose replicates did not all settle. The x axis is logarithmic automatically for runs of 1,000 generations or more ( fim sweep trajectories ). Error bars show Interval of the mean (95%, the default), Spread (standard deviation) across replicates, or Both . x scale and y scale are Automatic , Linear , or Log ; Automatic uses a log axis for a geometric series. Show theory adds the closed-form value for D , G ST , E ST , H S , and H T . With the chart focused

heading: Point health
text: Mark Meaning Drawn as healthy Every replicate settled and the interval meets precision Filled marker degraded Some replicates reached the generation cap, or the interval is wider than precision Hollow ring unreliable Every replicate reached the cap before settling Ring with an X A point that is not healthy is flagged, never omitted. The table's health column and the hover text give the reason.

heading: Continue, retry, and recompute
text: On Home, a Study that holds a sweep offers: Continue sweep: runs the points still missing ( fim sweep resume ). Retry failed (N): reruns only the failed points ( fim sweep resume --retry-failed ). Recompute all…: after confirmation, recomputes every finished point and compares it with its stored run, bit for bit ( fim sweep resume --rerun ). A match replaces the old run; a difference keeps both and writes reproducibility.json . Each opens the sweep's progress view. To compare two or more sweeps, see compare sweeps .

heading: Run names
text: Each point's run is named after the Study and its values, for example Migration and number of demes sweep m=0.001, d=8 . Its description locates it in the sweep: Point 8 of 21 of the sweep "Migration and number of demes": m=0.001 of m=[0.0001..0.1] (7 values); d=8 of d=[4, 8, 16]. A reused run keeps its existing name.

heading: Compare runs and sweeps
text: Comparison reads saved results. Nothing is rerun, and nothing is saved: reopening a comparison recomputes it.

heading: Compare runs
text: Choose Compare in the rail. Select two or more completed runs from the list ( Run , Ended , Outcome ), then choose Compare . The screen shows two overlays: Small multiples: one final-state scatter panel per run, deme 1 against deme 2. Panels name the parameters that differ between runs. Trajectory overlay: one statistic over generations, one color per run. Statistic selects D , G ST , E ST , K ST , H S , H T , or H ST ; switching redraws without another computation. Runs with different seeds, configurations, or retention are compared as saved. Check that differences in N, ploidy, or migration convention are intended before you interpret a difference; see implementation conventions .

heading: Compare sweeps
text: Start on Home, in either of two ways: Compare sweeps… on an Experiment's row compares the sweep Studies inside it. Select , tick sweep Studies from any Experiments, then choose Compare selected sweeps… . The comparison screen draws one curve per sweep, each with a distinct color and marker, over the axis you pick. Other shared axes are held at a value. It has the error-bar, scale, and theory controls of the sweep results screen; each theory curve uses its own sweep's settings. Degraded and unreliable points stay flagged. With exactly two sweeps, a second panel shows their difference (first minus second) with a 95% Welch interval and a zero line. That interval assumes the sweeps' replicates are independent. Two sweeps built from the same seed and grid share seeds point for point; the command-line fim sweep compare reports whether seeds were different, shared, or partly shared, and does not adjust for sharing. Sweeps can be compared only on axes they all vary, at values they share, and with the same ploidy. Otherwise the comparison is refused with the reason. See sweep a parameter for fim sweep compare .

heading: Home and organization
text: Home lists everything saved in your results folder: Experiments, the Studies inside them, their runs and batch replicates, and unfinished saved runs. Rows summarize report.json or summary.json ; batch results are reconstructed from their saved replicates.

heading: Experiments, Studies, and runs
text: An Experiment groups Studies; a Study groups runs. A run can belong to more than one Study and counts once in an Experiment. Default study and a default Experiment are created when needed. Configure files new runs in the Study selected at its foot. A Study's pooled results can combine runs with different parameters; a "varies across members" note identifies them. A Study that holds a sweep has sweep actions; see sweeps . Close freezes a group's membership; Reopen reverses it. A group cannot be closed while one of its runs executes, and closing never pauses or stops a run. The Examples experiment appears last.

heading: Names, descriptions, and documentation
text: Name Description Documentation Experiment Required One line, optional Longer notes, optional Study Required One line, optional Longer notes, optional Run Optional (the folder name stands in) One line, optional — Hover an Experiment, Study, or run name, in Home, the run view's title, Configure's Study choice, or a sweep screen, to see its description. Click the name, or the ⓘ beside it, to open the details dialog. Save keeps changes; Cancel , Escape, or a click outside discards them. An empty field clears the value. Create experiment… on Home and New study… in Configure take an optional description beside the name. Configure's Run name and Run description label the next run. The run view's title names the Experiment first, then the subject, for example Ring vs island — Baseline (run-20261005-101500-000000) , … — initial conditions (p₀) before a run, or … — in progress . Names, descriptions, and class are stored in metadata.json , beside manifest.json . They never change the manifest or the run ID. The command-line equivalents are --description and --documentation on fim study create and fim experiment create , and fim run --name and --description .

heading: Open, clone, and delete
text: Double-click a run to open its saved result. Expand a group to see its runs. Clone fills Configure with the run's parameters, Run name, and Run description. It does not change the source run or its Study. Loaded run settings follow the rules in loaded run settings . Select shows checkboxes; Select all , Clear selection , and Delete selected act on them. Confirmation names every run that a group deletion affects. A run that is still executing has no checkbox: pause, cancel, or stop it first. Opening a trajectory supports retained-generation analysis and differentiation-order ( q ) evaluation; see re-analyze a trajectory .

heading: Saved runs
text: Saved runs lists saved runs that have not completed, in any of the lifecycle states from draft to cancelled . Each row offers only the actions its state allows: Watch , Start , Resume , Resurrect , Clone , Edit , Cancel , Kill , and Delete . A row in transition refreshes every few seconds. Resurrect appears for a cancelled run whose latest checkpoint is verified and compatible. It continues exactly from that checkpoint. An unnamed saved run is listed by its settings, for example "225 diploid, d=10, m=0.01, mu=1e-05, 200 replicates". Hover the name for every setting, the object ID, and the run ID. Watch returns to the running view of a run this window executes. A run executing in another window or from the command line has no Watch . Completed runs move to the run list. Saved runs are shared with fim object ; a run created in the app can be paused or resumed from the command line, and the reverse. See saved runs: pause, resume, and recover .

heading: The Examples experiment
text: The Examples experiment holds the worked examples bundled with the app. Each example class is a Study (a nested class is named "Parent — Child"), holding that class's examples as runs with their saved results. The app writes them into an examples folder inside your results folder at startup, writes them again if they are removed, and replaces them when a newer version of the app ships new versions. An example whose result has not been saved is not listed here, but it is still available in the Examples… dialog. The examples and the questions each one addresses are described in worked examples .

heading: Read-only items
text: The Examples experiment, its Studies, and their runs are read-only . A lock beside the name marks them in Home, the details dialog, and the run view's title. You can open, view, compare, and clone them. You cannot rename, describe, document, or delete them, or change their membership; those controls are unavailable, and hovering one says why. Select all never selects a read-only item. A deletion that names one is refused as a whole: nothing is deleted. The command line refuses the same edits with an error naming the item. An example linked into an editable Study is different: its checkbox selects only that link. Delete selected removes the link, not the example or its results; the confirmation says the example is kept. Read-only status comes from _read_only ; only shipped examples use it.

heading: Opening a saved example
text: Double-click an example's row on Home, or choose Open saved result in the Examples… dialog. The complete finished run opens: statistics, messages, graphs, and the scrubber. No simulation runs. Large examples can take longer to open while their compressed trajectory is reconstructed; the trajectory is stored losslessly and needs no manual unpacking. Batch examples include every kept replicate and the batch summary. Load into Configure gives an editable copy; running it creates a new, editable result.

heading: Settings and saved preferences
text: Settings , at the top of the window, holds preferences and defaults for new configurations. Saved Settings never change existing results or a configuration you have loaded. To change one configuration's run settings, use Run settings… in Configure.

heading: Startup and display
text: At startup : Restore the last submitted configuration opens the configuration last started with Run simulation ; Restart from the starter configuration uses built-in model values. Both apply saved run settings, not those of the restored configuration. Default ploidy for new configurations; Ask me each time requires a choice in each configuration before it runs. Run card graph columns and Scatter plot points (marker style; alleles at the same coordinates are counted together). significant digits rounds displayed values only; saved files keep full precision. appearance : Follow system , Light , or Dark . The first-launch welcome panel offers Examples… or Start from scratch . File > New configuration uses starter model values and saved run settings, ignoring the last submitted configuration.

heading: Statistics shown
text: Statistics shown selects statistics for the statistics panel, results tables, trajectory chart, and sweep charts. Presets are Essentials , Differentiation , Nei distances , and Everything ; a filter box and checkboxes select individually. Choose… beside a statistics table opens this section directly. Final saved results include hidden statistics. Showing any of E ST , K ST , , , or I enables per-generation tracking of all five for new runs, which increases run time, especially with many demes. Hiding all five disables that tracking unless one is watched for convergence. See track_expensive_statistics . Save every deme pair for runs with up to N demes sets the pairwise.json limit (default 1024). The file grows with : about 0.5 MB at 100 demes and 52 MB at 1024, per run and per replicate. Above the limit no matrix is saved; any single pair can still be recomputed from the saved trajectory.

heading: Background work
text: These settings apply to jobs started after you save them. Run priority : Normal , Lower , or Lowest . Lowest can make simulations several times slower on macOS. The interface always keeps normal priority. Each job's effective priority appears in its tab. Keep CPU cores free : whole logical cores or a percentage, rounded up to whole cores. The worker budget is the remaining cores, at least one. Keep memory free : Automatic keeps the larger of 2 GiB and 10% of physical memory free; you can instead reserve GiB or a percentage. Before a job starts, the app estimates its added memory and asks if the estimate would cross the reserve. While work runs, a warning appears if available memory falls below the reserve; each listed job has a Pause button. Runs pause at a checkpoint; sweeps stop at a resumable point.

heading: Storage location
text: Storage location holds results, logs, and Study and Experiment data. Change… takes effect the next time you open fim . When a --root or --results-directory flag, or FIM_HOME or FIM_RESULTS_DIRECTORY , sets the location, the field is locked; change or unset that instead. See where results, logs, and preferences are written .

heading: Defaults for new configurations
text: These are the defaults that Run settings… starts from: execution engine , n_replicates , max generations , confidence , max workers , and max concurrent replicates ; under Convergence , convergence burn-in , precision , expected value , precision method , and replicate averaging window ; under Expert: engine tuning , JIT , auto-vector min d , and auto-vector max capacity ; and under Storage , trajectory retention , trajectory stride , and thinning start . Expert settings control convergence policy, statistical calculations, and storage. Their values are recorded in the manifest and contribute to the run's identity. Reset all to default restores the shipped values. See expert . Each control's meaning is in the configuration reference ; the correspondence is listed in run settings . max workers describes this computer, not the run, and never changes results.

heading: Where preferences are stored
text: Preferences hold defaults and interface state. They are not the record of a run; each run's configuration, seed, and results are in its own folder under results/ . Platform Location macOS ~/Library/Application Support/fim/preferences.json Windows %APPDATA%\fim\preferences.json Linux $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fim/preferences.json (usually ~/.config/fim/preferences.json ) --preferences-file or FIM_PREFERENCES_FILE overrides the location. If the file contains invalid JSON or an unsupported format, the next launch shows a dismissible banner and uses built-in defaults. The invalid file is kept as preferences.invalid-<timestamp>.json . Removing the preferences folder resets Settings without changing results/ .

heading: A result disagrees with a published value
text: Check, in order: Units of N: individuals × ploidy = gene copies. Migration convention: fim 's scalar m draws from the other demes; a redraw-from-all- d rate converts by . Estimand: population statistic, not a sample estimator; ratio of means across loci, not mean of ratios. Equilibrium: was the burn-in long enough, and did the run converge? See implementation conventions and the comparison protocol .

heading: A run takes very long or reaches the cap
text: Low migration or mutation can need tens of thousands of generations, or more, for the initial state to decay. The derived burn-in and cap appear beside Run simulation before you start. Reaching max generations is a valid, non-converged result; the report gives the precision achieved. Options: raise max generations , accept a larger precision , add independent loci, or use a batch. A batch can reduce elapsed time but not total computation, because each replicate has its own burn-in. See why does my run take so long?

heading: A run finished in a few hundred generations
text: Check whether convergence burn-in or max generations in Run settings… is a small fixed number, perhaps from a loaded configuration. Use auto for both unless you have a specific reason not to.

heading: Configure rejects a value
text: The app returns to Configure and marks the field. Press F1 in that field for its reference entry. A loaded YAML file with an unknown or misspelled key is rejected, never silently ignored; compare the key with the configuration reference .

heading: Memory warning
text: The app estimates each job's added memory before it starts and asks if the estimate would cross the reserve in Background work . While work runs, a warning lists jobs with Pause buttons when available memory falls below the reserve.

heading: Sweep messages
text: Another process is running this sweep: a sweep locks its Study. The lock is released when the other process exits, including after a crash. The stored sweep plan no longer matches: a newer release changed what a run ID covers. Run fim sweep replan STUDY_ID --dry-run , then fim sweep replan STUDY_ID . See sweep a parameter . A point failed: the sweep continues. Use Retry failed (N) on Home. A failure the engine reports is not retried automatically, because the same configuration fails the same way.

heading: An item cannot be edited or deleted
text: Examples are read-only . A deletion that includes a read-only item is refused as a whole. A run that is executing cannot be deleted; pause, cancel, or stop it first.

heading: Closing the window
text: When closing would lose something, fim asks first. That happens when a configuration has unsaved changes, a saved run is in progress (runs started with Run simulation are saved runs), or a sweep is in progress. The dialog lists every affected document, including tabs not on screen. Button Effect Save and close Saves configurations under Saved runs on Home (Draft if incomplete, Planned if valid), then closes Close without saving Discards unsaved changes and closes Pause and close Shown when only a saved run is active; it pauses at a checkpoint for later Resume Stop and close Shown when only a sweep is active; the sweep stops Keep working Leaves the window open Save and close and Close without saving also pause a running saved run or stop a running sweep. If saving fails, the dialog stays open with the reason. A sweep setup is not stored with a saved run. If a sweep setup was edited, Save and close saves the run configuration and keeps the dialog open with an explanation: Keep working retains the setup for this session; Close without saving discards it.

heading: If the window closes but fim keeps running
text: If shutdown has not finished 20 seconds after the window closes, fim records diagnostics and exits with status 3: fim: shutdown did not complete within 20s; forcing exit Completed results remain on disk. A saved run resumes from its latest checkpoint; work since that checkpoint may be repeated. The diagnostic report is written to logs/fim.log . Report the section that begins shutdown deadman fired , with your platform and launch method; see known issues . To investigate, set FIM_GUI_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT to a longer timeout in seconds, or 0 to disable the forced exit, before launching: FIM_GUI_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=0 fim --graphical

heading: Settings were reset
text: If preferences.json is invalid, the app shows a banner, uses built-in defaults, and keeps the invalid file as preferences.invalid-<timestamp>.json . See where preferences are stored .

heading: Logs and diagnostics
text: The app writes a rotated log to logs/fim.log under the storage location. A double-clicked app or fim --graphical accepts no logging flags; set FIM_LOG_LEVEL and FIM_LOG_OPTIONS before launching. They correspond to the command line's -l and -L . See the logging design and global flags .

heading: The app does not open on Linux
text: The app needs WebKitGTK, a system package most desktop distributions already include. See installation alternatives .

heading: fim configuration reference
text: fim run accepts one YAML mapping. Unknown keys, incompatible shapes, and out-of-range values are errors. See Using fim for commands and the project overview for installation. Mathematical quantities use ; YAML keys, literal values, and API identifiers use backticks. Display equations have unique local tags.

heading: Complete example
text: N: 225 ploidy: diploid d: 20 m: 0.001 mu: 0.0000003 seed: 20260814 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 200 initial_allele_count: 2 initial_concentration: 1.0 deme_weighting: equal convergence_statistic: D convergence_combinator: all precision: 0.01 max_generations: auto # derived from the model; see below n_replicates: 200 # the default: an adaptively stopped batch; 1 asks for a single run engine_backend: auto # recommended choice; the library default is lineal

heading: N
text: Type: positive integer, or a list of d positive integers Required: yes Meaning: individuals per deme N counts individuals per deme. The simulator multiplies it by ploidy to obtain the gene-copy count: N: 225 with ploidy: diploid is 450 gene copies per deme. That conversion happens once, when the configuration is read; everything after it, including every statistic and the analytic formulas, works in gene copies. Per-deme lists model unequal island sizes: every stage of the update pipeline ( migrate , drift , mutate ), the founding-allele-count bound (checked against the smallest N i ), and deme_weighting: size (when chosen) all use each deme's gene-copy count. N: [120, 450, 60] # three demes, unequal individual counts ploidy: haploid d: 3 A scalar N and a list of d equal values are numerically identical; prefer the scalar form when every deme is the same size.

heading: ploidy
text: Type: haploid , diploid , triploid , or tetraploid Required: yes Meaning: gene copies per individual (1, 2, 3 or 4) Specifies gene copies per individual. Use a named value, not a number. For example, N: 225 with ploidy: diploid represents 450 gene copies. Numeric ploidy values are rejected to prevent ambiguous interpretation of configurations that use N as a gene-copy count. N: 225 # individuals per deme ploidy: diploid # 2 gene copies each, so 450 gene copies per deme Literature configurations that state haploid reproductive individuals, such as Jost (2008) Part VI and the Dear-Nolan scenarios, say ploidy: haploid , so their individual and gene-copy counts are equal. Because it is part of the recorded configuration, two runs that differ only in ploidy get different auto-generated run ids, even when their gene-copy counts are equal: 450 haploid and 225 diploid individuals are the same genetic process but different recorded population descriptions.

heading: d
text: Type: integer at least 2 Required: yes Meaning: number of demes

heading: m
text: Type: number in [0, 1] , or a d by d row-stochastic matrix Required: yes Meaning: migration rate or complete migration weights A scalar uses the symmetric finite island model: each deme retains 1 - m of its frequency vector and receives m from the size-weighted average of all other demes. Matrix rows must each sum to 1. A full matrix models asymmetric migration — row k gives destination deme k 's source weights, and row k 's weights need not equal row j 's. Every row is independently configurable, including rows that are not symmetric with any other row. m: - [0.90, 0.05, 0.05] # deme 1 retains 90% and receives 5% from each neighbor - [0.10, 0.80, 0.10] # deme 2 blends evenly with both neighbors - [0.00, 0.20, 0.80] # deme 3 exchanges only with deme 2 d: 3 Matrix and scalar forms have the following relationship: A matrix's rows are the authoritative weights — they are not scaled by N . The scalar path automatically derives a size-weighted migrant pool from each deme's gene-copy count; a matrix directly specifies the destination's source mix, so N does not alter that blend. If unequal deme sizes should also drive migration weighting, build that weighting into the matrix itself. (Thi

heading: mu
text: Type: number in [0, 1] , or a list of exactly one rate per locus Required: yes, unless mu_b is given instead (the two are mutually exclusive) Meaning: per-gene-copy mutation probability per generation: after drift draws a deme's N new gene copies, each one, independently, mutates with this probability (the textbook Wright-Fisher model) A scalar applies identically to every locus, regardless of length , and is the right choice whenever every locus should mutate at the same rate. A list gives each locus a rate, positionally matched to loci : mu: [0.001, 0.01] loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 50 - locus_id: 2 length: 500 Deriving mu from a per-base rate mu specifies per-locus probabilities independently of length. Alternatively, mu_b specifies a shared per-base-pair mutation probability. Write for the probability configured by mu_b , for the positive integer length , and for the derived per-locus probability. Each base avoids mutation with probability ; all bases avoid it with probability . Taking the complement gives: (CFG.1) mu_b: 0.00003 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 10 # mu ≈ 0.0003 here - locus_id: 2 length: 8000 # mu ≈ 0.216 here — the same mu_b, a much higher mu This uses the full pro

heading: seed
text: Type: non-negative integer Required: yes; there is no default Meaning: seed for the run's NumPy PCG64 generator Negative seeds are rejected; there is no upper bound.

heading: loci
text: Type: nonempty list of mappings Default: one locus with locus_id: 1 and length: 200 Each entry has a positive length and an optional positive locus_id that defaults to its one-based position. IDs must be unique. As an alternative to loci , use: n_loci — positive locus count, default 1 ; locus_lengths — one positive integer shared by all loci, or exactly n_loci integers, default 200 . Do not combine the two forms. Differentiation statistics never read length directly; it acts only through the mutation model, below. Per-locus length varies freely — nothing requires every locus to share one value. loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 50 # a short marker - locus_id: 2 length: 8000 # a much longer one The equivalent compact form: n_loci: 2 locus_lengths: [50, 8000]

heading: mutation_model
text: Type: infinite_alleles or finite_alleles Default: infinite_alleles Controls what a mutation event turns an allele into , independently of mu (which controls how often one happens). infinite_alleles (the default): each mutation produces a globally unique label. This approximates mutation at a locus that spans many base pairs — see the differentiation-measures guide — but increasingly unrealistic for a short locus, where the same state can plausibly arise more than once by chance (a recurrence ). finite_alleles: each locus gets a bounded state space of exactly possible states, where is its length , corresponding to four bases per sequence position. A mutation target is drawn uniformly from the other capacity - 1 states — never its current state, but possibly one already present elsewhere in the run. This still imposes no ordering or distance between alleles; it only gives the label space a ceiling. See the simulator design, §3.2 and §9 for the assumptions and the distinction from a stepwise (microsatellite) mutation model, which is not implemented. mutation_model: finite_alleles loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 1 # capacity 4 — recurrence becomes likely quickly finite_alleles interacts wi

heading: Initial conditions
text: Generation 0 — whether drawn from initial_concentration or supplied explicitly via p_0 — is a continuous prior, not a state the run's N gene copies could themselves produce; only generation 1 onward, once drift has resampled at N gene copies, lands on that discrete 1/N lattice. See the model contract and simulator design §3.3 .

heading: initial_allele_count
text: Type: positive integer no larger than the smallest N Default: 2 Founding IDs are locus-relative 0 through initial_allele_count - 1.

heading: initial_concentration
text: Type: positive number Default: 1.0 The random default draws each deme/locus frequency vector independently from a symmetric Dirichlet distribution. Smaller values are more uneven, down to a value small enough that generation 0 itself lands arbitrarily close to fixation; differentiation statistics computed from a frequency table that close to fixation remain within [0, 1] rather than raising.

heading: p_0
text: Type: optional nested list: d demes, each containing one mapping per configured locus Default: absent Allele keys are integer IDs and each mapping must sum to 1. When present, p_0 is used verbatim instead of a Dirichlet draw. Newly mutated allele IDs are allocated above both the reserved mutation range and the highest supplied ID, so they cannot collide with explicit labels. p_0: - - 0: 0.75 1: 0.25 - - 0: 0.10 1: 0.90

heading: equilibrium_convergence_window, equilibrium_convergence_tolerance, equilibrium_max_generations
text: Type: integer of at least 2; number greater than 0; positive integer Default: absent (all three) Together these select the equilibrium-split starting condition instead of the Dirichlet draw above. Set all three, or none of them: a partial configuration is rejected. Equilibrium-split derives starting frequencies from a simulated ancestral population. First, one population holds the sum of all demes' gene-copy counts and undergoes drift and mutation without migration. After its model-derived equilibration period, it splits into d demes by sampling without replacement, allocating each deme its configured gene-copy count. This sampling introduces founder variation at generation 0. The first-phase duration is derived from the model, not detected from a flat trajectory. At equilibrium, population diversity ( H S , which equals H T when there is only one deme) fluctuates around its expectation. The model describes the rate at which dependence on the initial state decays. With ancestral gene copies and mutation rate , its approximate relaxation time is: (CFG.2) This is the same idea as Convergence defaults , for one deme. The first phase runs until the population's expected diversity, from

heading: convergence_statistic
text: Type: the name of any global statistic, or a list of several of them (the statistics the app lists under "Statistics shown", except the per-pair ones). Identity statistics: D , G_ST , H_S , H_T , H_ST , Gs , Gd , D_m , R_ST , G_ST_NEI_LOG , G_ST_HEDRICK , F_ST and the all-demes Nei identities and distances ( NEI_I_ALL_GEO , NEI_D_ALL_ARITH , and so on). Allele-spectrum statistics: E_ST , K_ST , A_CGD , Delta (Gregorius's ), MI (Sherwin mutual information). Default: [D, G_ST] By default a run watches both and stops when both have settled (convergence_combinator all ): D is the statistic most studies report, and G ST is the one that is slowest and noisiest at low diversity, so a run that has settled on D alone can still be imprecise on G ST . Name one statistic ( convergence_statistic: D ) to judge the run on it alone. Every watched statistic is computed every generation, whatever the display settings say. The allele-spectrum statistics are expensive (a pass over every allele per locus per generation) and are not covered by the relaxation time, which is derived for the identity statistics: they depend on allele counts and rare alleles, which can relax more slowly. The Expert Setting

heading: statistic_precision
text: Type: mapping of a watched statistic's name to its precision Default: none (every statistic uses precision , or the relative precision above) Gives one watched statistic a precision target in that statistic's units, replacing precision for it. The name must be a watched statistic and the value non-negative. In the app this is the optional "per-statistic precision" field under the convergence statistics on Configure, written A_CGD=0.5, D=0.02 . convergence_statistic: [D, A_CGD] precision: 0.01 statistic_precision: A_CGD: 0.5 # known to within half an allele

heading: convergence_combinator
text: Type: all or any Default: all Only meaningful when convergence_statistic is a list: all requires every watched statistic to be simultaneously stable before stopping (a strict criterion); any stops as soon as one settles. With a single watched statistic, the two settings are equivalent. The default watched set contains D and G_ST . Under any , the statistics that did not trigger the stop may still be imprecise when the run ends: their reported window means are not converged estimates. report.json 's converged_on names the statistics that had settled. Use all when every watched statistic's value matters.

heading: convergence_burn_in
text: Type: positive integer, or auto Default: auto The generations discarded before averaging starts: the time the population needs to forget where it started. Nothing can stop a run before its burn-in ends (except the cap), and generation 0 is never averaged. auto (the default) derives the burn-in from the model. How long a run must be watched depends on how fast the population forgets its starting state, its relaxation time tau : T = N_total + (d - 1) / (2 m) # mean time for two gene copies to coalesce tau = 1 / (2 mu + 1 / T) # mutation is a second way to lose identity burn_in = ceil(k tau), k = max(5, ln(2 / precision)) max_generations = max(200000, burn_in + ceil(15 tau)) N_total is the sum of every deme's gene copies and mu is the smallest mutation rate over loci (the slowest locus sets the time). That closed form is for the symmetric island model (scalar m , equal deme sizes). An explicit migration matrix or unequal sizes use the slowest mode of the identity recursion instead, computed for up to 24 demes. Above that, or with no migration and no mutation, there is no tau : auto then discards the first tenth of the run at each check, and a derived max_generations is refused, so giv

heading: convergence_estimate
text: Which expected value a run estimates for D and G ST , the two statistics that are functions of the heterozygosities H S and H T : Value Estimate Use it for mean_of_values (default) The average of statistic values over the evidence window Comparing with published replicate means value_of_means The statistic computed from the window's averaged H S and H T Checking the simulator against the closed form auto value_of_means when the statistic is undefined in any window generation, or its denominator is tiny in too many of them; otherwise mean_of_values Runs near fixation The two differ by a small, systematic amount (the average of a ratio is not the ratio of the averages); one locus at the reference scale shows 0.011 for D and 0.0001 for G ST . The choice drives the stopping decision, the headline number and the standard error. The report carries both forms for D and G_ST under window_statistics , with selected_form and undefined_generations . auto is judged at each check, so the form reported at the stop is the form the stop was judged on; it does not default because the headline would then change meaning between points of a sweep. The auto thresholds are the Expert Settings estimate_a

heading: precision
text: Type: non-negative finite number Default: 0.01 How precisely to estimate each watched statistic: plus or minus this amount, in the statistic's units, at the confidence level. The same target applies to single runs and batches. A single run burns in and then averages each watched statistic over a growing window until the average's standard error is at most precision / z ( z is 1.96 at 95% confidence) and the window holds at least 50 effective independent values. The burn-in also lengthens as the precision tightens (see convergence_burn_in). A replicate batch stops early once every watched statistic's across-replicate confidence interval is this narrow (see stop_batch_early). Smaller is more precise and takes longer. precision: 0.02

heading: track_expensive_statistics
text: Type: boolean Default: false Controls whether E ST / K ST / /Delta/MI are computed every generation for display, even when none of them is being watched for convergence. D, G ST , H S , and H T are always tracked and available for display regardless of this setting and regardless of convergence_statistic — each is either the shared H S / H T input every other statistic derives from, or an O(1) step once those are known, so computing them costs nothing extra. E ST , K ST , , Delta, and MI each require an additional pass over frequency tables. Enabling this setting computes all five every generation for live plots and tables, increasing runtime. The cost grows with deme and allele counts; omitting E ST and K ST reduced convergence-check time by about 38% in a many-allele reference configuration. Statistics named in convergence_statistic are always computed, regardless of this setting. Leave it false unless supplementary live histories are needed. See the statistics reference for definitions. track_expensive_statistics: true In the desktop app there is no control for this key on Configure. The app sets it on every run, batch and sweep it starts, and in every preset or YAML file it sav

heading: max_generations
text: Type: positive integer, or auto Default: auto This safety cap always ends a run. Reaching it is reported as a valid outcome that did not reach the requested precision, with the average and error bar the run has. auto derives it as max(200000, burn_in + ceil(15 tau)) , at most 10,000,000 (at least 200,000, so a single locus has room to average its variation down to the configured precision — see How precise is the reported value? ); see convergence_burn_in . A cap at or below the burn-in ends the run before any averaging, and the run logs a warning. Setting only a burn-in raises the derived cap to leave 15 tau after it.

heading: history_format
text: Type: exact or compact Default: exact A run keeps, for every generation, the value of each statistic ( D , G_ST , the heterozygosities): the statistic history that the app draws as the trajectory graph and that a sweep's trajectory view averages across replicates. exact writes it as convergence.jsonl , every value at full precision, about 70 bytes a generation. compact writes convergence.fhist instead: each value is rounded to a fixed step of about one hundredth of precision (a power of two, so a stored value is exact in binary), and the differences between successive generations are packed to the narrowest integer that holds them and compressed. A real 355,000-generation replicate takes 0.3 MB in the compact form and 25 MB in the exact one. At the default precision (0.01) a value is within 0.00002 of the one computed, far inside the interval the run is asked to resolve. report.json , summary.json and every reported number are computed inside the run and are never rounded. The setting is outside a run's identity and is recorded in manifest.json only for a compact run. Sweeps write the compact form unless asked otherwise.

heading: trajectory_retention, trajectory_stride, trajectory_thinning_start, trajectory_keep_last, trajectory_keep_burn_in

text: Type: ratio_of_means or mean_of_ratios Default: ratio_of_means Controls how D and G ST combine across loci in the final report, when more than one locus is tracked. heading: Convergence: burn in, then average
text: This guide describes how fim determines run completion and derives burn-in and generation-cap values from model parameters.

heading: If you only read one section
text: A run first completes a burn-in , the period during which the initial condition's influence decays. It then collects an evidence window until the estimated average reaches the requested precision ( precision at the specified confidence ). The report includes the estimated average and its uncertainty. If the generation cap is reached first, the run reports that status and the uncertainty achieved. A short run does not by itself demonstrate equilibrium. Check convergence_burn_in , max_generations , and the reported uncertainty against the model's timescale. There are two separate questions: Has the initial condition's influence decayed enough? Burn-in addresses this possible bias. Has enough evidence been collected to estimate the equilibrium average precisely? The averaging window and its error bar address sampling uncertainty. A long burn-in does not automatically answer the second question. A small error bar does not repair a burn-in that ended too early. The population need not stop changing for its equilibrium average to be estimable.

heading: Why does my run take so long?
Interpretation
text: Population structure changes over generations through migration, mutation, and drift. Low migration can produce long relaxation times, often tens of thousands of generations. Drift continues to cause generation-to-generation variation at equilibrium; the evidence window estimates the average to the requested precision. Set convergence_burn_in and max_generations to auto to use the model-derived values. The app displays the expected burn-in next to the Run simulation button before execution, for example: Convergence: burn-in 104,338 generations, cap 399,728 (derived; this model needs about 19,693 generations to forget its starting state) If a run reaches the cap before meeting its precision criterion, the report gives the achieved uncertainty. Possible responses include increasing the generation cap, accepting a wider interval, adding independent loci, or using multiple replicates. Parallel execution can reduce elapsed time, but each replicate incurs its own burn-in, so a batch need not reduce total computation.

heading: Checking the numbers yourself
text: dev/bin/relaxation-table prints the identity operator's gap timescale beside the scalar approximation and the migration gap for six reference models. The unit tests in test_defaults.py fail if the closed form is off by more than 5%. test_burn_in_monitor.py pins the schedule (burn-in, first check, doubling) and the stop rule on exact series, and test_window_statistics.py checks the estimator against hand-worked values and known autoregressive series. test_convergence_rule_calibration.py checks committed calibration evidence and seeded scenarios, including Golden Part VI and the Dear-Nolan low example. Its slow checks exercise the combined simulation and stopping rule. test_convergence_docs.py checks that the documented burn-in and cap formulas contain the shipped policy constants, including their rendering here. These checks address different claims. Matching the table verifies the policy calculation; matching an analytic covariance series verifies an estimator; matching an equilibrium simulation adds scientific evidence for the combined system. None substitutes for the other two. Fixed-seed checks can be reproduced without rerunning until a favorable sample appears.

heading: Limits
text: Each limit links back to its main explanation; that explanation also links here so the qualification can be read in context.

heading: Scalar approximation limit
text: The scalar closed form is an approximation for the equal-size symmetric island model, checked within 5% of the identity operator in the reference tests. It is not an exact discrete-generation formula for all parameter values. Return to units and the scalar island approximation .

heading: Matrix and size limit
text: Unequal sizes do not merely substitute their sum into that scalar formula. They use the size-weighted scalar migration matrix or the explicitly supplied matrix and the identity eigenproblem, provided . An explicit matrix is not reweighted by sizes. Larger cases needing that route require explicit run limits and cannot receive this model-derived timescale. Return to the choice of timescale calculation . The flattened operator derivation explains why the eigenproblem grows so quickly.

heading: Slowest-locus limit
text: The slowest locus is selected by its smallest mutation rate within this identity approximation, not by observing that every possible statistic has settled. Return to the mutation-rate choice in the scalar approximation .

heading: Empirical-cap limit
text: The 200,000 floor is measured from two regimes, not derived from first principles. A third, faster-mixing regime needed far less (12,000), so the floor has real margin, but a configuration not yet measured could need more before its precision is reached, in which case the run reports the cap honestly, with the average and error bar it has, rather than a false convergence. Return to the safety-cap calculation .

heading: Check-scheduling limit
text: Checks occur at approximately doubled window lengths, not every generation, to keep checking cheap. If precision first becomes adequate between checks and remains adequate, the next check can require nearly twice as much evidence, apart from integer endpoint effects. Estimated precision need not improve monotonically. Return to window boundaries and check scheduling .

heading: High-migration evidence limit
text: The Dear-Nolan high-migration scenario (100 demes of 2,000 gene copies) is not covered by the cited replicated measurement; at that measurement's backend and hardware it cost about 0.4 seconds per generation. That is not a current cross-backend performance guarantee. Its scalar timescale is dominated by mutation (about 499 generations). The dense 100-deme recursion exceeds the implementation guard, so that scale should not be described as a fresh direct eigensolver check. Return to the scalar timescale and its calculation routes .

heading: Finite-alleles limit
text: The finite-alleles mutation model changes the mutation term and is not covered by the infinite-alleles derivation: independent mutations can produce matching labels. A timescale supplied by the current defaults must therefore be read as a heuristic for that model. Return to the drift-and-mutation identity derivation .

heading: Stochastic-migration limit
text: Stochastic migrant amounts also need a second-moment qualification. Conditional on a realized mixing matrix, (C.30) applies, but averaging generally requires , not . In particular, the two weights for a same-deme pair share a random migrant fraction. The defaults do not build that augmented second-moment operator; do not interpret their timescale as an exact recursion for this variant. Return to the two-parent migration-weight derivation .

heading: Finite-evidence limit
text: A constant or apparently stationary evidence window can miss rare transitions. The error bar is conditional on the stationarity and correlation assumptions used to estimate it. Increasing the effective-count floor cannot prove those assumptions. Return to the autocorrelation estimator and its cutoff .

heading: Allele-label stationarity limit
text: Infinite-alleles stationarity refers to frequency structure and statistics modulo allele relabeling. Absolute newly assigned allele IDs keep increasing when mutation continues; those labels do not have a stationary registry distribution. Return to what the pairwise identity table measures .

heading: Saved runs: pause, resume, and recover
text: A saved run (a "Run object") stores a configuration for later execution and supports pausing and continuation from a checkpoint, including after a computer restart. This guide explains what you can do with a saved run, what each state means, and how to recover when something goes wrong. Return to the command reference or the project overview .

heading: Quick start
text: In the desktop app: choose Run simulation to create and start a Run object automatically. heading: Checkpoints and exact continuation
text: A checkpoint is the complete state of the simulation at one generation: the population, the random number generator, the convergence monitor, and the committed position in the trajectory log. A run writes one: at generation 0, as soon as the run is set up; every 1,000 generations or every 60 seconds, whichever comes first; whenever it pauses. Resuming is exact. A run that is paused or cancelled and resumed, any number of times, produces the same trajectory, the same report, and the same convergence decision as a run that was never stopped. A trajectory log cut off by a crash is trimmed back to the checkpoint and continued from there. Cancellation may leave logs beyond the checkpoint too; resurrection discards those frames and recomputes them exactly. Replicate artifacts are rewritten at completion, and unneeded replicate folders are removed. Log block encoding and its manifest digests can differ after reopening; the decoded trajectory and scientific results are identical. A checkpoint's SHA-256 digest is verified before use. Incompatible checkpoint format versions are rejected.

heading: Cost of a checkpoint
text: On an Apple M4 laptop, a single replicate with and takes about 20–35 ms per checkpoint and keeps about 350 KB on disk. A 16-replicate vector-engine batch with large d takes about 135 ms per checkpoint and keeps about 19 MB. Only the latest checkpoint is kept, so disk use does not grow with run length.

heading: Compatibility between versions
text: Versions without saved-run support ignore results/objects/ . They cannot see or resume saved runs. A run.json with a schema_version this version does not know is refused with unsupported run.json schema_version . A checkpoint from a different checkpoint format version is refused, not converted. Run the configuration again from generation 0 with fim object clone OBJECT_ID .

heading: Continuing from another run's checkpoint
text: A run is a pure function of its configuration: the same settings and seed always produce the same trajectory. A planned object can therefore continue from the checkpoint of any stopped object with the same configuration digest, instead of recomputing those generations. $ fim object start obj-7c… --continue Copying the checkpoint of obj-36b1… Continuing from generation 4000 of obj-36b1… Starting obj-7c… obj-7c… is completed at generation 30000 --continue alone picks the matching object furthest along; --continue SOURCE_ID names one. Put it after the object ID. Without --continue , start names a matching object when one exists, and then starts from generation 0 as asked. A source qualifies when it has the same configuration digest and run kind, has a checkpoint, and is paused , interrupted , failed , or cancelled . A running or completed object is never a source. The checkpoint and its trajectory logs are copied (as copy-on-write clones where the file system supports them), verified against their recorded digests, and only then installed. A copy that does not verify is discarded and the object stays planned . The object records the adopt-checkpoint event and becomes paused at the sou

heading: Recovery after a crash or power failure
text: Each command that reads objects ( list , status , start , resume ) first checks every object recorded as running. When no process owns it any more, the object is recorded as interrupted , and fim object resume continues it from its latest checkpoint. If every final artifact was written but the last lifecycle update was lost, the command verifies the completion receipt and records the object as completed without rerunning it. A command killed in the middle of writing can leave a hidden staging folder (its name starts with . ) next to the run. These folders are never mistaken for real data. fim object reclaim --dry-run lists them, and fim object reclaim removes the ones no running command owns.

Cancelling a sweep pauses the points in flight; fim sweep resume STUDY_ID resumes them from their checkpoints instead of starting them over. Only a completed point counts as finished. Use a Run object for work that may need to continue across sessions. Supported configurations. Every engine backend ( lineal , generational , and generational-vector ) supports saved runs. A configuration is refused at start, with the reason, when: it asks for the JIT on the lineal backend; it asks for generational-vector and Numba is not installed; a locus exceeds the vector backend's capacity.

heading: Troubleshooting
text: "… cannot resume; fim object clone … saves its configuration as a new run". The run stopped before its first checkpoint, so there is nothing to resume. Clone it and start the clone. "another attempt is executing run object …". Another process owns the run: a second terminal, the desktop app, or a sweep. Pause it there, or wait for it. A run whose owner has gone (killed, crashed) is never blocked: the next command records it as interrupted . "config.yaml of … no longer matches its recorded configuration digest". The saved config.yaml was changed by hand after the run started. A run never continues with a configuration it did not start with. Restore the file, or clone the object and start the clone. status reports a damaged artifact. A file in the object folder no longer matches its recorded digest. Check the disk, then clone the object and run it again. Disk full while running. The run fails at its next write and keeps its latest checkpoint. Free space, then fim object resume OBJECT_ID . Hidden folders beginning with . next to runs. These are leftovers from killed commands. Run fim object reclaim .

Who this document is for

Every comparison of this kind needs a mapping between two independently chosen sets of conventions before the numbers mean the same thing; get the mapping wrong, or skip it, and an entirely correct simulator and an entirely correct paper can disagree substantially while both sides are right (§2.1).
