heading: The one-paragraph version
text: The statistics commonly grouped under "differentiation" quantify different properties. The classical family ( G ST , F ST , ) is related to the reduction in within-population variation. Jost's D , entropy differentiation E ST , and allele-count differentiation K ST quantify separation among allele-frequency distributions in other ways. The values need not covary: a parameter set can produce a high value for one family and a low value for another. Under the finite-island model and the mutation assumptions analyzed in the paper, equilibrium nearness to fixation depends on Nm , whereas equilibrium D depends on , where is the mutation rate and d is the number of demes. These relationships apply to the stated infinite-time mutation-migration-drift equilibrium. Away from that setting, including finite-allele mutation models and short timescales with negligible mutation, population size, elapsed time, and the allele model can affect the results directly. See the finite-island model introduction for the process model. The project-wide statistics reference maps names to definitions and result identifiers.

heading: Genes, loci, and alleles
text: An organism's genome is a long string over a four-letter alphabet ( A , C , G , T ) — think of it as a very long array of characters, copied, with rare errors, from parent to offspring. A locus (plural loci ) is a region of that array — a contiguous interval, fixed by where it starts and how far it runs. It says where to look , never what is found there. A locus may span a single character or a run of thousands. An allele is a value that can occupy that region — the whole sequence a given copy carries across the interval, read as one indivisible label. If some individuals carry AAGCT over a five-character locus and others carry AAGGT , those are two alleles of that locus. A gene is a locus whose sequence codes for something functional. Whether a locus is a gene or not changes no formula in this paper — it affects the biological interpretation of the result. The analogy that survives the whole document: a locus is a field , an allele is a value that field can hold , and a population is a collection of records . Every measure discussed here is a statistic computed from the histogram of values in one field, across a collection of records. Alleles are treated throughout as unordered ca

heading: Distance between alleles is a different model
text: An allele label can be given a metric in a different model, and then mutation becomes something like a transition in a space of sequence states. That is a perfectly sensible model for sequence divergence or evolutionary distance , but it is not the model used here. The paper is not asking, "How far apart are these allele labels in a sequence or mutational metric?" It is asking, "How different are the frequency distributions of the labels across demes, and how much of the variation is unique to one deme rather than shared across them?" The metric space model and the categorical-label model answer different questions. For a sequence-space model, one typically needs additional structure: a way to compare allele labels to each other, a mutation model that says how one label turns into another, and usually a distance or similarity matrix that depends on the biology of the locus. With that extra structure, one can define actual genetic distance, pairwise sequence divergence, or a diffusion-like mutation process in a continuous or discrete state space. In that setting, mutation really is a transition in a state-space, and distance can matter very much. This paper deliberately does not cho

heading: Diploidy, homozygous, heterozygous
text: Most organisms of conservation interest are diploid : each individual carries two copies of every locus, one from each parent. Homozygous at a locus: the two copies are the same allele. Heterozygous at a locus: the two copies are different alleles. A group of N diploid individuals therefore contains gene copies at any given locus. That factor of 2 is the only reason and keep appearing in the formulas below; it carries no conceptual weight.

heading: Populations and demes
text: A population is all the individuals of one species in the area of interest. A deme (or subpopulation) is a sub-group that mostly breeds within itself — an island, a mountain valley, a forest fragment cut off by a highway. "Mostly" does real work: demes usually still exchange a trickle of individuals. The paper uses d for the number of demes and N for individuals per deme. Habitat destruction takes one large interbreeding population and shatters it into small, isolated demes; each small deme then loses variation quickly (see drift, below). Whether that loss is recoverable depends on whether the fragments still hold different variants — exactly the question these statistics answer.

heading: The only state variable that matters here
text: For a single locus in a single deme, the complete state used by every formula in this document is a probability vector : the list of allele frequencies. Deme Allele frequencies 1 A: 0.70, B: 0.25, C: 0.05 2 A: 0.10, D: 0.90 Entries are non-negative and sum to 1 within each deme. It is worth being precise about why they sum to 1, because the reason is narrower than it first appears. The normalization runs over gene copies at one locus , not over the genome: each of the deme's copies carries exactly one sequence across the interval, so the alleles are mutually exclusive and exhaustive per copy , and their frequencies partition the copies. This holds locus by locus and asks nothing whatever of any other locus — not disjointness, not independence, not a carving of the genome into loci. Two deliberately overlapping loci would each still have frequencies summing to 1; you would be double-counting the shared characters, but neither vector's normalization would break. Independence across loci is a genuine requirement, but it buys something else entirely: the right to combine loci — averaging G ST across many markers to estimate Nm , taking harmonic means of D and , and attaching confidence

heading: The forces that move allele frequencies
text: Between one generation and the next, a deme's frequency vector changes under up to four processes; only the first three appear in this paper's models. Genetic drift is finite sampling noise. The next generation's gene copies are drawn from the current pool; whichever alleles happen to get drawn more often become more common, for no reason at all. This is a random walk with absorbing boundaries at 0 and 1. Two properties matter: Drift is stronger in small demes — the variance of the frequency change per generation scales roughly as . Drift is irreversible in aggregate : it always erodes variation within a deme, because 0 and 1 are absorbing. Left alone, every deme eventually ends up with a single allele. Migration (gene flow) replaces a fraction m of a deme's gene pool each generation with arrivals from elsewhere. Migration pushes demes towards each other , counteracting drift's tendency to make them differ. Since m is a per-generation proportion, Nm is roughly the number of migrant individuals per generation. Mutation introduces brand-new alleles at rate per locus per generation. Mutation is the only source of new variation — drift and migration only redistribute what already exist

heading: Fixation
text: A deme is fixed at a locus when every gene copy in it is the same allele — the frequency vector is a one-hot vector. All internal variation at that locus is gone; only mutation or immigration can restore it. This word is the hinge of the whole paper. Two facts to hold onto: Fixation is a property of one deme in isolation . A deme is fixed or it is not; the question does not mention any other deme. Whether two demes are fixed for the same allele or for different alleles is a completely separate question. The older family of statistics answers question 1 (averaged across demes). The newer family answers question 2. Conflating them is the error this paper exists to correct.

heading: Markers: what actually gets measured
text: Researchers rarely sequence whole genomes for this purpose. They pick markers — loci that are cheap to type — and hope those markers represent the genome. SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism): one character position, so at most 4 alleles and in practice usually 2. Cheap, abundant, very low . Microsatellite : a short repeated motif whose repeat count varies, e.g. CACACACA… . Many alleles, very high . Historically the workhorse marker of this field. MHC loci and similar functional genes: not neutral, directly tied to fitness (disease resistance, in the MHC case). Expensive but, the paper argues, the ones that ought to drive decisions. The gap between "the fast-mutating marker that was measured" and "the functional locus that is actually of interest" becomes decisive in Part VI: allelic differentiation depends strongly on , so a marker with a very different mutation rate from the locus of real interest gives a very different answer.

heading: Part II — Measuring diversity inside one group
Expected heterozygosity
text: Given one deme's frequency vector , the standard diversity statistic is expected heterozygosity : (J.1) Interpretation: draw two gene copies at random, with replacement, from the deme's pool. is the probability they are the same allele, so H is the probability they are different . The name comes from diploidy — under random mating, H is the fraction of individuals expected to be heterozygous at that locus. Statisticians will recognize it as the Gini–Simpson index; information theorists as one minus the collision probability; ecologists call the same quantity Simpson diversity. Range and behavior: exactly when the deme is fixed. H increases with more alleles and with more even frequencies. always, and only as the number of alleles . That last point is the seed of the whole problem. The two building blocks: H S and H T

heading: Part V — Classical measures and their limitations
text: The "98% within demes" reasoning above is standard, and the paper states flatly that every step leading to it is mathematically and biologically incorrect. Here are the steps, separately.

heading: The ceiling argument
text: A short proof with large consequences. Since always, (J.49) So if within-deme heterozygosity is , then G ST cannot exceed 0.05 — no matter what . The demes could share no alleles. They could be different species, incapable of interbreeding at all. G ST still cannot exceed 0.05. This makes nonsense of the common habit of reading G ST against a fixed verbal scale ("below 0.05 is negligible structure, above 0.25 is strong"). With high-diversity markers such as microsatellites — chosen because they are informative — the entire upper range of G ST is mathematically unreachable. At the descriptive level this behavior is, the paper stresses, correct : a population with low really is far from fixation, and G ST is a nearness-to-fixation measure. The defect lies entirely in the interpretation people give it.

Shannon entropy really is additive this way — heterozygosity is not ; it is subadditive. The correct partition into independent within- and between-group components (Jost, 2007), with equal deme weights, is: (J.50) Solving for the between-group component gives: (J.51) which is exactly the first bracket of D . So: D is nothing more than the correctly-partitioned between-group component of heterozygosity, normalized onto . It is not a rival index invented to compete with G ST — it is what falls out of doing the partition correctly instead of incorrectly. heading: The replication principle
text: The deeper requirement, and the reason effective numbers are mandatory before taking ratios: if a diversity measure is to be compared as a ratio , it must be linear under pooling of equally large, equally diverse, completely distinct groups . Pool two groups that share nothing and are equally diverse, and the measure must double . Testing both candidates on species C from above (20 private alleles per deme, two demes, nothing shared): (J.52) (J.53) Heterozygosity moved by 2.6% where the true diversity doubled. Any ratio taken on the H scale is therefore meaningless, and "98% of diversity is within demes" is an artifact of the scale rather than a fact about the population. This replication principle is the axiom underpinning Jost's whole research program across ecology, genetics, and phylogenetics.

heading: D also has a ceiling, and that one is honest
text: For balance: D has a range restriction too. When the number of alleles is fewer than the number of demes, D cannot reach 1.00. But this is not the same kind of defect. With 3 alleles and 10 demes, the pigeonhole principle guarantees some demes share an allele — so they are not completely differentiated, and a measure of actual allelic differentiation should report less than 1. The constraint is a true fact about the data. G ST 's ceiling is different in kind: it depends on H S , a property of within-deme diversity that has nothing to do with how much the demes actually share.

heading: Equilibrium assumptions in conservation applications
text: The paper cautions against using the equilibrium relationships to infer current migration. Neither G ST nor D should be used to estimate current migration , common practice in conservation genetics until recently. Present-day values reflect an accumulation of historic and recent migration and population sizes; populations that are now completely isolated can still show a low G ST simply because isolation has not yet had time to leave its mark. Threatened populations are, by definition, not at equilibrium — they are of concern precisely because their deme numbers, sizes, and migration rates have recently changed, and bottlenecks and fragmentation do not have to be recent to still be distorting these statistics. D is somewhat more robust here, since it is independent of within-group diversity and therefore more stable against variation in deme size, but past variation in migration rate still leaves a mark on it too. The paper's own recommendation follows from this: work at the descriptive level, measuring present-day magnitudes of D , E ST , and K ST at the loci of actual interest, rather than making inferences based on unverifiable equilibrium assumptions.

Absent that generative process, there is no , m , N , or equilibrium, and none of those formulas means anything. G ST and the whole fixation family. heading: Appendix E: the differentiation debate, 2008–2011
text: The 2008–2011 exchange over G ST and D is best read not as a contest over which formula is numerically larger on a given dataset, but as a dispute over which question addressed by an analysis. One question is how close demes are to fixation; another is how different their allele compositions are. The classical and Jost families address different quantities, a distinction discussed in the 2008–2011 exchange. Jost's position. In the 2008 paper, Jost argued that the classical G ST family, and by extension many uses of F ST and , was being interpreted as if it measured absolute genetic differentiation when it in fact measured the opposite: the degree to which a population has moved toward fixation within the pooled array. The formal point was not trivial. The classical family normalizes by H T , while the allelic family normalizes by . Those are different denominators, and therefore different concepts. Once this is acknowledged, the apparent paradoxes in the paper's worked examples are no longer paradoxes at all: a population can be nearly fixed within demes and yet retain almost no common allele content across demes, producing a very low G ST and a very high D . heading: The short version
text: Nei's distance compares how often two gene copies match between demes with how often they match within demes. Zero means the demes are alike; it grows as they diverge. It is infinite when the selected identity rule yields zero. The denominator (the "within" part) can be a geometric mean (Nei's 1972 original) or an arithmetic mean (the version Jost uses). The arithmetic-denominator distance is never smaller; the two agree exactly when the demes are equally diverse. Pair forms compare the two demes chosen for the scatter plot. All-demes forms summarize every deme at once. With several loci, Nei's own rule combines loci first and takes one ratio (the default). The per-locus mean takes one distance per locus and averages them. The all-demes geometric form can be negative . That is not an error; it means within-deme diversity is very uneven across demes. See When the distance is negative . Every form is computed and saved for every run. Choose which ones to see in Settings, "Statistics shown"; the Nei family starts hidden.

text: A negative value does not mean the demes are "closer than identical". It means the question this form asks, "how does typical between-deme sharing compare with the geometric mean of within-deme sharing", is being dominated by a few very diverse demes. heading: 1. Why scientists model population differentiation
text: An important question in population genetics is: how genetically different are two or more populations of the same species? The answer matters in several ways: Conservation. If two frog populations are genetically almost identical, losing one is a setback. If they are strongly differentiated, losing one destroys variation that cannot be recovered from the other. Taxonomy. Whether two plant populations are different varieties or different species often turns on exactly this question. Evolutionary biology. Watching differentiation build up over time shows how quickly isolation turns one population into two lineages. Answering it quantitatively takes two separate pieces of machinery: A model of the process that produces genetic differences between populations over time. This is the island model, the subject of this document. A statistic computed from observed or simulated data that reports the extent of differentiation. Lou Jost's D is one measure proposed for quantifying differentiation alongside the classical F ST and G ST family. heading: 2. Wright's island model: the starting point
text: The finite island model is a variant of a much older and simpler model due to Sewall Wright (1931, 1943), usually just called the island model . Understanding the plain version first makes the word "finite" easy to place.

heading: 2.1 The setup
text: There are d separate subpopulations, called demes or, by metaphor, islands, each holding a fixed number N of individuals. Most species of conservation interest are diploid — each individual carries two copies of every gene, one from each parent — so each island holds gene copies at any one location in the genome. Time moves in discrete, non-overlapping generations : generation t is entirely replaced by generation . There is no smooth, continuous change to track — only a sequence of discrete snapshots, each produced from the one before it by a fixed rule. Each generation, a fraction m of each island's gene pool is replaced by migrants. In the classic island model, those migrants come from an infinitely large, well-mixed pool that represents the average allele frequency across all the other islands combined. Mathematically, this means the source that supplies migrants never itself changes through drift or depletion — it behaves like a fixed, external reservoir that never runs low or shifts composition. After migration, each island rebuilds its population by drawing gene copies at random from its own (post-migration) local pool. This drawing step is where genetic drift happens: with o

heading: 2.2 Finite versus infinite migrant reservoirs
text: In Wright's original formulation, only the individual islands are finite in size ( N each); the total collection of all islands that supplies migrants is implicitly infinite — migrants always arrive from a fixed background frequency that itself never drifts. This assumption permits a simple closed-form formula for the equilibrium value of F ST , because the migrant source does not change through drift. Wright also analyzed the finite subgroup case directly. In Isolation by Distance (1943), he wrote the model with K subgroups of size N and derived the finite-deme sampling correction before giving the familiar large N , small m approximation. Later finite-island work did not invent the finite deme count from scratch; it extended Wright's setup to multiple alleles, mutation models, and higher moments. The finite island model used here is that finite-subgroup version. There are only a finite number of islands, d , each of finite size N , and no infinite external reservoir standing behind them. Migrants in generation t are drawn from the actual, finite, currently-drifting collection of all the other islands' current frequencies. Three consequences follow: The whole set of islands togeth

heading: 3. The model as a repeating random process
text: Set aside islands and alleles for a moment. The mechanics of this model are easiest to see as an ordinary repeating process: a set of numbers gets updated by a fixed rule involving some randomness, once per tick, over and over.

heading: 3.1 What is being tracked
text: At generation t , the complete state of the model is a table of allele frequencies — one row per island, one column per possible allele at the genetic location being tracked: d is the number of islands, distinct from Jost's statistic D . k is the number of distinct alleles possible at that location. is the frequency (a number between 0 and 1) of allele j on island i at generation t . Every row sums to exactly 1: (I.1) For a location with only two possible alleles (a "SNP," short for single nucleotide polymorphism, the most common type of genetic marker in modern studies), and the whole row compresses to one number per island, since the second allele's frequency is always 1 minus the first. Other markers, especially the short repeated-sequence markers called microsatellites , can have many alleles — k in the range of 5 to 20 is common — which is one reason Jost's statistics are built to generalize cleanly past the two-allele case, unlike some of the older F ST variants.

The stepping-stone model (a different, spatial relative, easily confused with the island model in casual reading). is the frequency of only the islands that are physically adjacent — a one- or two-dimensional lattice of islands exchanging migrants only with their neighbors. heading: 3.3 Variations found in the literature
text: Mutation. With some small probability each generation, each newly drawn gene copy can change its allele's identity outright, independently of every other copy (the textbook Wright-Fisher model; fim applies it after drift, to the copies drift has just drawn). This matters for studies of long-run equilibrium between mutation, migration, and drift; it usually is not needed for simulations covering only a few dozen or a few hundred generations from a defined starting point, where migration and drift alone dominate the outcome. Unequal island sizes. Letting N vary by island changes both the drift step (each island draws its own copies) and the weighting used to build the migrant pool . Unequal or asymmetric migration. Letting the migration rate m vary by island, or specifying a full matrix of pairwise migration rates between specific island pairs, generalizes the model into what is sometimes called a general migration-matrix model; the plain island model is the special case where every rate is the same. Selection. Not part of the base model, which assumes every allele is neutral — meaning no allele carries any survival or reproductive advantage over another. Neutral markers remain the c

heading: 4. Software implementations and scope
text: Several tools implement discrete-time population-genetic models with migration and drift. Their state representations, migration models, and outputs differ. quantiNemo 2 , from Jérôme Goudet's lab (Neuenschwander, Michaud & Goudet, Bioinformatics , 2019, DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty737 ; source at github.com/jgx65/quantinemo ), is an individual-based, forward-time population-genetics simulator for structured populations connected by migration, configured through a text settings file. Its C++ implementation provides individual-based and population-based modes. hierfstat , an R package also from Goudet's group (source: github.com/jgx65/hierfstat ), includes functions — sim.freq.t , sim.genot.t , and the more general sim.freq.metapop.t — that simulate the discrete-time migration-plus-drift process described in Part 3, generation by generation, with an arbitrary migration matrix, including stepping-stone layouts. The fim package also implements finite-island migration, drift, and mutation with per-generation statistic histories. Its Python API guide documents programmatic simulation, and the generated API reference lists the public Python symbols. The model design describes the upda

heading: 5. Reading Lou Jost's papers with this model in hand
text: The following publications develop and evaluate differentiation statistics in population-genetic models. Bibliographic details and DOI links are provided for each cited work. Jost L, "$ G_{ST} $ and its relatives do not measure differentiation." Molecular Ecology 17(18):4015–26, 2008. DOI: 10.1111/j.1365-294x.2008.03887.x . PMID: 19238703. The foundational critique. In the language of Part 2: under the finite island model, as the diversity within a population goes up, the maximum possible value G ST can reach — even at complete differentiation between islands, meaning zero shared alleles — goes down , sometimes sharply. A highly diverse marker showing might represent complete differentiation, while a low-diversity marker showing the same 0.2 represents only mild differentiation. The statistic is therefore not directly comparable across markers or studies with different diversity levels (see also the Fixation index discussion of the upper-bound issue: "the interpretation of F ST can be difficult when the data analyzed are highly polymorphic ... F ST can have an arbitrarily low upper bound"). Jost proposes D , defined to isolate the differentiation component independent of within-pop

heading: Appendix A: relation to statistical mechanics
text: Optional. This appendix uses concepts from statistical mechanics, including symmetry groups and mean-field models. The finite island model's coupling structure — each island's next state depends on a weighted combination of some set of other islands' states, plus a random local update — resembles what physicists call a Markov random field. One question is whether it can be described as a Markov random field whose local variable lives in some continuous rotation group — for some n — with allele frequency playing the role of a continuous angular/positional variable, the way a spin lives on a circle or sphere in an -symmetric physics model. A related question is what actually is the symmetry group of the finite island model, given that some kind of discrete transform seems to be involved? The coupling-structure analogy holds up well, but no continuous rotation group survives as an exact symmetry of the model itself. It helps to separate three different questions: the graph structure of who is coupled to whom; the ambient continuous symmetry that appears when the model is transformed into a more convenient coordinate system; and the actual symmetry group of the physically constrained s

heading: Appendix B: relation to ancestry inference
text: Optional. This appendix uses mixture models, likelihood methods, and population-structure inference. The finite island model's state representation—discrete groups, each with its own allele-frequency vector, and individuals drawn from those frequencies—is related to standard statistical clustering techniques. The allele-frequency table treated here as simulated ground truth (Part 3) is an unknown parameter inferred by some population-genetics tools from observed genetic data. The direct connection: STRUCTURE and its descendants. Pritchard JK, Stephens M, Donnelly P, "Inference of population structure using multilocus genotype data." Genetics 155(2):945–59, 2000. heading: Using fim
text: This guide covers commands and output files. The desktop app has its own desktop app guide , also bundled in the app. See what this simulates for the model, the configuration reference for parameter types and defaults, and the statistics reference for definitions, interpretation, and implementation links. Return to the project overview for installation and documentation links. Mathematical quantities use ; configuration keys, report identifiers, and commands use backticks. Display equations have unique local tags.

heading: Create a configuration
text: fim init [--output PATH] [--force] fim init writes the documented development scenario. N is individuals per deme and ploidy says how many gene copies each carries, so N: 225 with ploidy: diploid is 450 gene copies. Without --output , the path is project-root/results/example-run.yaml , where project-root is the root of this checkout when you are running from one, a fim folder in your home directory for the packaged desktop app, and otherwise (a plain pip install , run from a terminal) your current working directory. Existing files are protected unless --force is present.

heading: Run a simulation
text: fim run CONFIG [-o DIRECTORY | --output DIRECTORY] [--quiet] [--workers N] [--sequential] [--max-concurrent-replicates N] [--pairwise-max-demes N] CONFIG is a YAML file described in configuration.md . Without --output , a timestamped directory is created under project-root/results/ . The timestamp affects only the folder name and manifest metadata; it never affects the trajectory, statistics, convergence decision, or deterministic run_id. --pairwise-max-demes N (default 1024) is the largest deme count for which the run saves every deme pair's statistics in pairwise.json . The file grows with the square of the deme count: about 0.5 MB at 100 demes and 52 MB at 1024, per run and per batch replicate, and about a second to write at the largest size. Above the limit the file records only that the matrices were skipped; any single pair can still be recomputed from the saved trajectory, which the desktop GUI does on demand. --quiet suppresses progress and artifact-path messages. Validation errors name the offending key or value and return status 2. A run that reaches max_generations also returns status 0 because it is a valid, inspectable non-converged result.

heading: Why does my run take so long?
text: Low migration or mutation can require tens of thousands of generations for dependence on initial conditions to decay. A run first discards a burn-in, then averages until its stopping rule is satisfied. convergence_burn_in and max_generations default to auto , derived from migration, mutation, and population sizes; explicit values override them. fim run prints the derived values unless --quiet , and the desktop app shows them next to Run simulation before you start. For five islands of 100 gene copies with m: 0.0001 and mu: 0.000001 that is a burn-in of about 104,000 generations. A 100-generation run cannot provide an equilibrium estimate for that configuration. The derivation and evidence are in Convergence ; the settings are in configuration.md .

heading: Batches (n_replicates greater than one)
text: A config's n_replicates (see configuration.md ) controls whether one run or a whole batch executes: n_replicates: 1 : scalar-run artifacts directly in the output directory. n_replicates greater than one (the default: 200 , with stop_batch_early and a precision of 0.01 usually stopping well short of it) : each replicate gets a replicate-NNN/ subdirectory containing scalar-run artifacts, plus a batch-level manifest.json and summary.json — see Output schemas . Omitting n_replicates selects a batch with an across-replicate confidence interval. Set n_replicates: 1 for a single run. The fim init configuration states n_replicates: 200 explicitly. Most worked examples use batches; examples of within-run behavior use one replicate. A batch runs under any engine_backend , not only lineal ; every backend writes the same replicate-NNN/ + manifest.json + summary.json layout. Backend parity follows the documented engine_backend rules: lineal , generational and generational-vector produce the same trajectory, bit for bit, for the same seed on the same machine, so running the same batch under a different backend reproduces every replicate (and across different machines, statistically — the compile

heading: Save, pause, and resume a run
text: fim run runs to the end in one go. For a run you may need to stop and continue later, save it as a Run object instead: fim object create my-run.yaml # draft if invalid, planned if valid fim object start OBJECT_ID # runs in the foreground fim object pause OBJECT_ID # from another terminal: stop at a checkpoint fim object resume OBJECT_ID # continue exactly where it stopped fim object list # every saved run and its state A resumed run reproduces an uninterrupted run. Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, a crash, or a power failure loses at most the work since the last checkpoint (1,000 generations or 60 seconds). The desktop app's Save for later and Saved runs use the same objects. See saved runs: pause, resume, and recover for every state, command, and recovery case. Sweep setup is not stored with a saved run. If you edit a sweep setup, Save and close saves the run configuration but keeps the close dialog open with an explanation. Choose Keep working to retain the setup in the current session, or Close without saving to discard that setup. Saving the run configuration alone does not clear the sweep's unsaved-edit warning.

heading: Worked examples
text: Each example below is a complete config and the command that runs it: save the YAML, run the command, and the reported values match those shown here, because the same seed, parameters, and version always give the same report.json on the same platform (see Reproduce a run ). Most use model-derived burn-in and generation caps ; timing examples use fixed averaging windows. Several use looser precision (0.02–0.05) or eight pooled loci to limit runtime. Their READMEs document the trade-offs and measurements. Runtime depends on backend, hardware, and workload. Single-locus results can vary widely; use replicates to estimate the mean and its uncertainty. Each example uses a seed distinct from fim init 's starter config. Each configuration starts with its labels ( name , description , class ) and _read_only: true , which protects the bundled copy; delete that line in an editable copy (see Run labels ). Each demonstrates one option, or one natural pair of options, from the configuration reference ; studies can combine them freely. In the desktop app , you do not need to copy the YAML: click Examples… on the Configure screen (or on the welcome panel the first time the app opens). The Example

heading: Unequal island sizes with a migration hub
text: Four demes of very different size, connected by an explicit d x d migration matrix rather than one shared rate — a small "hub" topology where deme 4 is both the largest and the best-connected: name: Unequal islands with a hub description: >- Three small islands and one large, well-connected hub island, joined by an explicit migration matrix. class: migration _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: [200, 200, 200, 800] ploidy: haploid d: 4 m: - [0.95, 0.02, 0.02, 0.01] - [0.02, 0.95, 0.02, 0.01] - [0.02, 0.02, 0.95, 0.01] - [0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.97] mu: 0.001 seed: 20260819 # Eight independent loci, pooled: one locus alone swings too widely for its # D to settle honestly (see the README). loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 - locus_id: 2 length: 100 - locus_id: 3 length: 100 - locus_id: 4 length: 100 - locus_id: 5 length: 100 - locus_id: 6 length: 100 - locus_id: 7 length: 100 - locus_id: 8 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D # Thinned storage: every generation up to 5,000, then one in ten, so the saved # trajectory is a fraction of the size; the statistics and the report are # unaffected. trajectory_retention: thinned traj

heading: Stepping-stone (spatial) migration
text: Six demes arranged on a ring, each migrating only with its two neighbors — specified through a named topology rather than all 36 matrix entries: name: Stepping-stone migration description: >- Six islands on a ring, each exchanging migrants only with its two neighbors. class: migration _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 150 ploidy: haploid d: 6 m: topology: ring rate: 0.05 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260819 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D precision: 0.02 # looser than the 0.01 default: about a minute fim run stepping-stone.yaml --output results/stepping-stone --quiet The batch of 16 replicates takes under two minutes and gives an average D of 0.146 ± 0.019 across replicates. precision: 0.02 keeps the batch short; the default 0.01 would take about four times as long (see the example's README ). Swap topology: ring for linear to remove the wrap-around edge between deme 1 and deme 6. In the GUI, the completed-run Literature visualizations panel includes an isolation-by-distance plot whenever the migration graph has at least two distance classes.

heading: Literature distance statistics from an explicit founder split
text: Three demes start with partially shared alleles at different frequencies. Migration shares alleles, mutation creates private alleles, and drift changes their abundance and survival. Compare Caballero-García-Dorado allelic distance (presence/absence), Gregorius (frequency distance), and Sherwin mutual information I ( MI ; information about population membership) with D and G ST . The split is imposed, not simulated from an ancestral population. All five measures are watched, so the stopping verdict applies to all of them. track_expensive_statistics also records the other supplemental measures. In the desktop app that flag follows Settings' Statistics shown ; watched statistics are computed regardless. Show , , and I there to see their trajectories. name: Allele sharing after a founder split description: >- Follow partially shared founder alleles as migration, mutation, and drift reveal the differences between presence, frequency, and information measures. class: statistics-and-convergence _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 100 ploidy: haploid d: 3 m: 0.02 mu: 0.005 seed: 20260914 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 p_0: - - 0: 0.8 1: 0.2 -

heading: Equilibrium-split founding
text: This example derives generation-0 frequencies from a shared ancestral population rather than specifying them directly or using independent Dirichlet draws. The ancestral population undergoes drift and mutation for a model-derived equilibration period, then splits into demes by sampling without replacement. Sampling introduces founder variation at generation 0: name: Equilibrium-split founding description: >- Islands founded by splitting one ancestral population that has already settled. class: mutation-and-founding _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 200 ploidy: haploid d: 3 m: 0.005 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260916 # Eight independent loci, pooled, and a looser precision for the main run: # one locus here needs about 30,000 generations to settle (see the README). loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 - locus_id: 2 length: 100 - locus_id: 3 length: 100 - locus_id: 4 length: 100 - locus_id: 5 length: 100 - locus_id: 6 length: 100 - locus_id: 7 length: 100 - locus_id: 8 length: 100 equilibrium_convergence_window: 20 equilibrium_convergence_tolerance: 0.01 equilibrium_max_generations: 2000 # the derived burn-in is 1,256 generations engine_backend: auto

heading: Stochastic migrant counts
text: By default, migration blends each deme's frequencies with an exact rate * N fraction of its neighbors' — a deterministic step given that generation's frequencies. migrant_sampling: stochastic instead draws the migrant count from , where N is the gene-copy count and r the migrant fraction, adding variation in migrant number: name: Stochastic migrant counts description: >- Draws each generation's number of migrants at random instead of using a fixed fraction. class: migration _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 100 ploidy: haploid d: 4 m: 0.05 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260819 migrant_sampling: stochastic loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D fim run stochastic-migrants.yaml --output results/stochastic-migrants --quiet The batch of 11 replicates takes about two minutes and gives an average D of 0.082 ± 0.010 across replicates (the model's expectation is 0.059, which the average of D's values sits above; see the example's README ). Re-run with migrant_sampling removed (or set to continuous , the default) at the same seed to compare against the deterministic-migration baseline directly. That batch gives an av

heading: Finite-length alleles (the K-allele model)
text: By default (mutation_model: infinite_alleles), every mutation receives a globally unique identity — the standard population-genetics idealization for a locus long enough that two independent mutations essentially never land on the same state. finite_alleles instead bounds a locus to states, where is the locus's length , and lets a mutation recur to one already present elsewhere in the run. This example uses a 3-base locus ( states) and high mu to make recurrent mutation likely: name: Finite-length alleles description: >- A three-base locus with only 64 possible alleles, so mutations can recur. class: mutation-and-founding _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 100 ploidy: haploid d: 3 m: 0.02 mu: 0.02 seed: 20260819 mutation_model: finite_alleles initial_allele_count: 2 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 3 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D precision: 0.02 # looser than the 0.01 default: under a minute fim run finite-alleles.yaml --output results/finite-alleles --quiet The batch of 20 replicates takes about twenty seconds and gives an average D of 0.602 ± 0.019 across replicates ( precision: 0.02 is twice the default plus-or-minus, wh

heading: Wright-Takahata finite-deme correction
text: Wright's finite-island model and Takahata's multiallelic identity treatment carry an explicit finite- d correction. This example keeps d small enough that the correction matters; increasing d while holding N , m , and mu fixed moves G ST toward the infinite-island approximation. name: Wright-Takahata finite-island correction description: >- Eight islands, few enough that the finite-island correction to G_ST matters. class: statistics-and-convergence _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 500 ploidy: haploid d: 8 m: 0.003 mu: 0.0002 seed: 20260914 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: G_ST precision: 0.02 # looser than the 0.01 default: under a minute fim run finite-deme-correction.yaml \ --output results/finite-deme-correction --quiet The batch of 10 replicates takes about nine minutes and gives an average G ST of across replicates ( precision: 0.02 keeps the batch short; see the example's README ). The closed-form finite-deme prediction for these parameters is about 0.141, below the corresponding infinite-island approximation of about 0.238 because the d / (d - 1) correction is retained. A single loc

heading: Kimura-Weiss isolation by distance
text: A 20-deme ring gives enough graph-distance classes for the GUI's isolation-by-distance panel to show the short-distance decay pattern from Kimura and Weiss. The run is still small enough for an interactive example, but large enough that distances 1 through 10 exist on the ring. name: Kimura-Weiss isolation by distance description: >- Twenty islands on a ring, where near neighbors are more alike than distant islands. class: migration _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 200 ploidy: haploid d: 20 m: topology: ring rate: 0.05 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260914 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D precision: 0.05 # looser than the 0.01 default: seconds, not hours # Thinned storage: every generation up to 5,000, then one in ten, so the saved # trajectory is a fraction of the size; the statistics and the report are # unaffected. trajectory_retention: thinned trajectory_stride: 10 trajectory_thinning_start: 5000 fim run kimura-weiss-isolation-by-distance.yaml \ --output results/kimura-weiss-isolation-by-distance --quiet The batch of 10 replicates takes about six minutes and gives averages and across replicates. p

heading: Per-base mutation rate across unequal locus lengths
text: mu_b (mutually exclusive with mu ) configures a single per-base-pair mutation probability . Each locus derives its mu from its length , written , through: (U.2) The exponent is the number of bases that must all avoid mutation. name: Per-base mutation rate description: >- One per-base mutation rate gives a 50-base and a 500-base locus different mutation rates. class: mutation-and-founding _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 150 ploidy: haploid d: 3 m: 0.02 mu_b: 0.00002 seed: 20260819 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 50 - locus_id: 2 length: 500 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D precision: 0.03 # looser than the 0.01 default: under a minute fim run mu-b.yaml --output results/mu-b --quiet The batch of 10 replicates takes about a minute and gives an average D of 0.199 ± 0.014 across replicates (the window is sized from the slowest locus, the 50-base one, so it is long enough to leave the approach from the starting state; precision: 0.03 keeps the batch short; see the example's README ). results/mu-b/manifest.json 's parameters.mu records the two derived rates — 0.0009995 for the 50-base locus and 0.0099503 for the 500-base one — th

heading: Several convergence statistics
text: Watch more than one statistic and decide whether stopping needs every one of them stable (convergence_combinator: all, the default) or one ( any ). In the desktop app this is the "stop the run when" pair of radio buttons at the foot of Configure's "convergence statistic(s)" panel, shown once two or more statistics are checked. Choose any with care. The run stops as soon as one watched statistic is stable and precise, so the others may still be trending or imprecise at that moment: their reported values and trailing-window means are then not converged estimates, only snapshots. all waits for every watched statistic. With one watched statistic the two are the same. name: Several convergence statistics description: >- Watches D and G_ST together and stops when either one settles. class: statistics-and-convergence _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 150 ploidy: haploid d: 3 m: 0.02 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260819 loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: [D, G_ST] convergence_combinator: any n_replicates: 1 # single run: this example is about one run's own stopping rule (`convergence_combinator: any`) fim run mul

heading: Within-run sigma band
text: A run burns in and then averages; everything after the burn-in is its evidence window. The report gives, for the window, both the precision of the average (the standard error) and generation-to-generation variation (the standard deviation, ). The across-replicate confidence interval in the next example instead measures uncertainty in a mean across independent replicates: name: Within-run sigma band description: >- Shows how much D still varies from one generation to the next once the run has settled, as a band over the evidence window. class: statistics-and-convergence _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 150 ploidy: haploid d: 4 m: 0.02 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260916 # Eight independent loci, pooled: one locus alone drifts close to fixation # for long stretches, where D looks deceptively steady (see the README). loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 - locus_id: 2 length: 100 - locus_id: 3 length: 100 - locus_id: 4 length: 100 - locus_id: 5 length: 100 - locus_id: 6 length: 100 - locus_id: 7 length: 100 - locus_id: 8 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D # Thinned storage: every generation up to 5,000, then one in ten, so the sa

heading: An adaptive replicate batch with a confidence interval
text: Set n_replicates as an upper limit and let precision determine when the across-replicate interval is narrow enough: name: Adaptive replicate batch description: >- Runs replicates, up to 50, until the confidence interval for D is narrow enough. class: replicates-and-engines _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 100 ploidy: haploid d: 5 m: 0.01 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260819 # Eight independent loci, pooled, and a loose precision: a single locus is so # noisy that each replicate would need tens of thousands of generations (see # the README). loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 100 - locus_id: 2 length: 100 - locus_id: 3 length: 100 - locus_id: 4 length: 100 - locus_id: 5 length: 100 - locus_id: 6 length: 100 - locus_id: 7 length: 100 - locus_id: 8 length: 100 engine_backend: auto convergence_statistic: D precision: 0.03 # plus or minus, for the batch's interval across replicates # Thinned storage: every generation up to 5,000, then one in ten, so the saved # trajectory is a fraction of the size; the statistics and the report are # unaffected. trajectory_retention: thinned trajectory_stride: 10 trajectory_thinning_start: 5000 n_replicates: 50 replicate_m

heading: A large- d batch under generational-vector
text: Every example above names engine_backend: auto , the recommended choice and the desktop app's starting value for a fresh form. auto never resolves to lineal (the library default): it picks generational or generational-vector (see engine_backend ), which reproduce lineal bit for bit for the same seed, so each example's committed output matches lineal ( test/validation/test_examples_auto_backend.py checks this by rerunning each example on lineal ). This example and the next explicitly select their backends. Each performs fixed work: 16 replicates, a one-generation burn-in, and a 99-generation averaging window, with stop_batch_early: false . These are timing workloads, not equilibrium estimates. generational-vector keeps a dense, array-native representation of every active replicate at once, and is the fastest measured choice once d grows large enough — see choosing an engine backend for the measurements motivating this workload: name: Large-d batch, vector engine description: >- A short 16-replicate timing workload with 70 islands under the generational-vector engine. class: replicates-and-engines _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 500

heading: A long-locus batch under the generational engine
text: The same batch shape as the example above, but favoring locus length over deme count instead — d: 35 with a 7-base locus (16384 possible allele states under finite_alleles ) rather than d: 70 with a 5-base one — and the generational engine. Benchmarks favor this backend in regions with moderate d and longer loci: name: Long-locus batch, generational engine description: >- A short 16-replicate timing workload with 35 islands and a seven-base locus under the generational engine. class: replicates-and-engines _read_only: true # marks the shipped copy read-only; delete it in your own copy N: 500 ploidy: haploid d: 35 m: 0.05 mu: 0.001 seed: 20260916 mutation_model: finite_alleles migrant_sampling: continuous loci: - locus_id: 1 length: 7 engine_backend: generational convergence_statistic: D # A fixed 100-generation horizon: each replicate burns in for one generation, # averages for 99 more, and stops, whatever its noise (a fixed window, no # precision check). convergence_burn_in: 1 replicate_averaging_window: 99 n_replicates: 16 stop_batch_early: false # always run all 16 replicates fim run generational-showcase.yaml --output results/generational-showcase --quiet Ran in about 35 second

heading: Sweep a parameter
text: A sweep runs one configuration over a range of one or more parameters and keeps every point as an ordinary run inside one study. A sweep file is a normal configuration plus a sweep: block: N: 450 ploidy: haploid d: 20 m: 0.001 mu: 0.0000003 seed: 20260814 n_replicates: 200 sweep: name: Migration and number of demes axes: m: { start: 0.0001, stop: 0.1, count: 7, scale: log } d: [4, 8, 16] Each axis is a list of values or a start , stop and count range ( scale is linear or log ). Any setting that is one number, one word or one on/off switch can be swept: the common ones are N , d , m , mu , topology ( island , ring , linear , torus ) and deme_weighting , and the rest include n_loci , locus_lengths , initial_allele_count , mutation_model , migrant_sampling , ploidy and precision . A switch takes true and false . Settings that are lists or groups ( p_0 , mu_b , loci , expert ) and seed (the sweep sets seeds, see below) cannot be swept. fim sweep keys lists every key with its type and legal values ( --json for a program). A point whose settings do not fit together is reported by plan , not discovered while the sweep runs. Nm is the number of migrants per deme per generation. Use it to h

heading: Re-analyze a trajectory
text: fim stats TRAJECTORY [--manifest PATH] [--generation N] [--q ORDER ...] [-o PATH | --output PATH] The default manifest is manifest.json beside TRAJECTORY . The final generation is analyzed unless --generation selects another persisted generation. Repeat --q to evaluate several Hill-number differentiation orders without re-running the simulation: fim stats run/trajectory.tlog --q 0 --q 1 --q 2 JSON is printed to standard output. --output also writes the same result. --q 0 and --q 2 match the report's K ST and D ; --q 1 matches E ST using the recorded deme_weighting . See differentiation measures for the Hill-number family and statistics for implementation links.

heading: Check for updates
text: fim update --check This explicit command queries the latest GitHub Release and prints its download page when a newer version exists. It does not download or modify anything. This is the application's only network path; run , stats , and init are offline.

heading: Desktop GUI ( fim-gui )
text: fim-gui The desktop app renders local HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the operating system's native web view. It uses the same simulation functions and results/ folder as the command line. python -m pip install . provides both fim and fim-gui . Packaged executables open the GUI with no arguments: double-click fim-windows-x64.exe or fim.app , or run fim-gui / fim --graphical on Linux. The desktop app has its own guide, bundled offline in the app under Help > Desktop help : the desktop app guide . heading: Global flags
text: fim --help fim --version fim -l debug run myrun.yaml fim -l info -L file=none run myrun.yaml --version comes from the same version.txt value used by packages, manifests, and release tags. -l / --log LEVEL ( debug , info , warn , error , or critical ; default warning ) and -L / --log-options KEY=VALUE[,KEY=VALUE]... control the operational log, independently of run --quiet and progress/artifact messages above. Every run already writes a rotated log file at project-root/logs/fim.log by default, whether or not -l / -L is given at all; -l debug raises what reaches it (and the terminal), -L file=none turns the file off entirely. Both flags must appear before the subcommand name ( fim -l debug run ... , not fim run ... -l debug ). Full flag reference, every -L key, and where each log call in the source lives: operational logging design . --logging-config PATH (or the FIM_LOGGING_CONFIG environment variable) replaces -l / -L entirely for one invocation, reading a standard-library logging.config.dictConfig YAML file instead — for a setup beyond the inline -L options (several loggers, several handlers, a custom formatter). It is not combined with -l / -L : the selected configuration replace

heading: Where results, logs, and preferences are written
text: By default, fim writes into results/ / logs/ in a source checkout, or a fim/ folder in your home directory for a packaged build (see operational logging design §6). Four flags, each with a matching environment variable, override this independently of one another — every one must appear before the subcommand name, the same as -l / -L above: Flag Environment variable Overrides --root PATH FIM_HOME Both results/ and logs/ at once, unless a more specific flag/variable below also applies -R / --results-directory PATH FIM_RESULTS_DIRECTORY Where runs, batches, Studies, and Experiments are written --log-directory PATH FIM_LOG_DIRECTORY Where fim.log is written --preferences-file PATH FIM_PREFERENCES_FILE Desktop preferences.json (form defaults, named presets, Settings); affects GUI launches fim-gui (the separate desktop-app entry point) accepts the identical four flags directly. For fim --graphical or a double-clicked build, set matching environment variables before launching, as with FIM_LOG_LEVEL / FIM_LOG_OPTIONS . Settings additionally provides a Storage location field for results; see storage location .

heading: trajectory.tlog
text: The run's trajectory, as a compact binary log: every nonzero allele frequency of every generation, most generations stored as only what changed since the one before. You rarely open it yourself; the app and fim stats read it directly. To get the text form ( trajectory.jsonl , below), export it: fim export results/my-run The trajectory log explains the size, what happens when a run is interrupted, how to export, and the file format.

heading: trajectory.jsonl
text: Produced only by fim export , from trajectory.tlog . One JSON object per nonzero frequency, byte for byte what json.dumps writes with sorted keys: {"allele_id":0,"deme":1,"frequency":0.5,"generation":0,"locus_id":1,"run_id":"run-example"} Field Type Meaning run_id string Deterministic identity for one parameter set and seed generation integer Generation, beginning at 0 deme integer One-based deme number locus_id integer Configured positive locus identifier allele_id integer Opaque identity-only allele label frequency number Positive allele frequency

heading: equilibrium_trajectory.tlog
text: Written only by an equilibrium-split run: the ancestral trajectory, simulated before splitting into your demes, as a binary log like trajectory.tlog . Every generation of that ancestral phase is kept. Its rows (export it with fim export to see them as equilibrium_trajectory.jsonl ) have exactly the trajectory.jsonl fields above, so anything that reads the trajectory reads this file too, with two differences: deme is always 1: the ancestral population is one deme holding all of your demes' gene copies. generation counts the ancestral phase separately, from 0 (the starting draw) to the manifest's equilibrium_generation_count . Its last generation is the population that was split. The main run's generation 0 in trajectory.tlog is the moment after that split, so ancestral generation g happened equilibrium_generation_count - g generations before it. The file has the same run_id as the main trajectory, and the manifest records its digest as equilibrium_trajectory . Runs with any other starting condition do not have this file.

heading: manifest.json
text: The manifest records the complete parameter mapping, seed, software version, UTC start/end timestamps, generation, watched statistic, and whether convergence or the hard cap ended the run. It also carries: schema_version : manifest format version. convergence.generation_count : number of generations stored in trajectory.tlog . With full retention this is convergence.generation + 1 ; thinning reduces the stored count. artifacts : the SHA-256 digest and byte count of trajectory.tlog , report.json , scatter.png , and every other file the run wrote (for example equilibrium_trajectory.tlog ) as they existed at the moment the run finished writing and flushing them. fim stats recomputes and checks the trajectory's digest (and its generation count) before reading a single row, so a trajectory edited, truncated, or replaced after the run completed is refused with a clear error rather than re-analyzed silently. output_directory (scalar-run artifacts, or the replicate-NNN/ plus summary.json / manifest.json tree for a batch) is built in a hidden temporary location beside the target path and published with a single atomic rename only once every file in it is flushed and manifest.json has been w

heading: report.json
text: The final report contains: run identity, generation, convergence flag, watched statistic, and reason; H S , H T , and the correctly partitioned H ST ; G ST ( null only when every tracked locus is fixed for the same allele in every deme; under per-locus ratio averaging, undefined loci are excluded rather than replacing defined values); Jost's D , entropy differentiation E ST , and allele-number differentiation K ST ; literature-derived supplemental statistics: Caballero-García-Dorado allelic distance , Gregorius ( Delta ), and Sherwin mutual information I ( MI ); the within- and between-deme gene identities G s ( Gs ) and G d ( Gd ); Nei's (1973) D m ( D_m ) and R ST ( R_ST ), Nei's logarithmic ( G_ST_NEI_LOG ), Hedrick's standardized ( G_ST_HEDRICK ), and coancestry F ST ( F_ST ), each computed from the pooled H S / H T and null where undefined; Nei's genetic distance across all demes in four forms, and the matching identities: NEI_D_ALL_GEO , NEI_D_ALL_GEO_LOCUS_MEAN , NEI_D_ALL_ARITH , NEI_D_ALL_ARITH_LOCUS_MEAN , NEI_I_ALL_* (see Nei distances ). A distance is null when infinite; its identity is always a number. A report.json may lack statistics added after its software version.

heading: pairwise.json
text: Every pair of demes' Nei identities and pairwise F ST at the run's final generation, so any pair can be compared later or analyzed outside fim . Written for every scalar run and every batch replicate, and digested in the manifest. { "schema_version": 1, "generation": 1234, "deme_count": 4, "mode": "full", "encoding": "upper-triangle-row-major", "matrices": { "NEI_I_PAIR_GEO": [0.91, 0.87, 0.80, 0.93, 0.85, 0.88], "NEI_I_PAIR_GEO_LOCUS_MEAN": [], "NEI_I_PAIR_ARITH": [], "NEI_I_PAIR_ARITH_LOCUS_MEAN": [], "F_ST_PAIR": [] } } (The empty lists stand for lists of the same length.) Each list is the upper triangle of a symmetric matrix, row by row: pairs (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4) for four demes, numbered from 1 as everywhere else in fim . The diagonal is not stored (identity 1, F ST 0). Each distance is for its identity I ; a pairwise F ST is null where undefined (both demes fixed for the same allele). With more demes than --pairwise-max-demes , "mode" is "skipped" , the limit is recorded as "max_demes" , and there are no matrices.

heading: Nei distances
text: fim reports Nei's genetic distance with the geometric-mean denominator and with the arithmetic-mean denominator (Jost, L. (2026) private communication), for the pair of demes the scatter plot shows and across all demes, combining loci by Nei's rule or by averaging per-locus distances. In the desktop GUI the forms start hidden: choose them in Settings, "Statistics shown", or with "Choose…" in the statistics panel's caption. The pair rows name the pair they describe and follow the scatter plot's deme selectors, live, after the run, and while scrubbing. Two results need a word of explanation: ∞ means the demes share no allele, so the identity is 0. A negative all-demes geometric distance is not an error. That form divides the average between-deme identity by the geometric mean of the within-deme identities, which one very diverse deme can drag far down. It signals strongly unequal within-deme diversity: compare the arithmetic form beside it, which stays non-negative, and the within-deme diversity ( H S , effective number of alleles). Pair forms and arithmetic forms are never negative. The arithmetic all-demes distance equals for Jost's D . Nei distances in fim has the full explanation

text: : direct Deme 1 versus Deme 2 scatter with a diagonal reference. : direct three-dimensional scatter. : every pairwise deme projection. : direct Deme 1 versus Deme 2 scatter, same as — not a PCA projection. One point represents one (locus, allele) pair. Coincident points are enlarged and annotated. What the marker colors mean Color identifies the most frequent allele in each displayed deme: Color Meaning Blue The most frequent allele in either of the two demes shown Orange Every other allele There are two blue points when the demes have different most-frequent alleles, and one when they share the same most-frequent allele. For ties, only the first allele is marked. The choice is deterministic and stated in the legend. Blue indicates a frequency maximum, not statistical significance or a frequency threshold.

heading: Batch summary.json and manifest.json
text: Written only for n_replicates greater than one, alongside the replicate-NNN/ subdirectories, each of which holds the scalar-run files above. summary.json maps each reported statistic name (every global statistic in report.json : D , G ST , E ST , K ST , H S , H T , H ST , , Gregorius , Sherwin's I ( MI ), G s , G d , the pooled-heterozygosity measures and the all-demes Nei forms) to its across-replicate confidence interval: { "D": { "mean": 0.643, "half_width": 0.021, "low": 0.622, "high": 0.664, "sample_std": 0.133, "sample_count": 40, "confidence": 0.95 } } half_width and sample_std describe different sources of uncertainty: half_width is how precisely the average is known — the "± 0.021" half of a "0.643 ± 0.021" report. Running more replicates shrinks it. sample_std is how much the replicates themselves differ from one another. Running more replicates does not shrink it, because it describes run-to-run variability rather than measurement of it. sample_std can be null for intervals built by resampling rather than the Student's-t formula ( fim.engine.bootstrap_replicate_summary ). Resampling intervals can be asymmetric; use low and high rather than assuming bounds of mean ± half_

heading: Reproduce a run
text: Copy manifest.json . Use its parameters object as a new YAML config. Run the same fim version shown in software_version. Compare trajectory.tlog and report.json byte for byte on the same platform. Desktop logs are canonicalized on close; if canonicalization reports a failure, compare exported trajectory.jsonl instead. Across software versions. One configuration and seed give the same result, bit for bit, every time within a software version (checked for single runs and for batches, run sequentially and in parallel). A run records the version that made it, and a run is only reused, by Run or by a sweep, when that version matches the current one. A configuration whose only run came from another version is recomputed, and the new run is compared with the old one using the digests each run records for its trajectory, report and summary (the scatter image is left out, since its bytes can change without any result changing). If they match, the old run is replaced by the new one and you are told. If they do not match, a warning names the values that changed, both runs are kept, and the difference is written to reproducibility.json beside the new run. fim sweep reports the difference and e

heading: Troubleshooting
text: Unknown key: compare the named key with configuration.md ; typos are never ignored. Output already exists: select a new output directory. fim refuses to publish into one that already exists at all, even if empty — never appended, overwritten, or reused. Reached the cap: the message names how many generations the model needs to forget its starting state. Inspect the trajectory and report, then increase max_generations, ask for less precision (a larger precision ), or select another convergence statistic based on the study's needs. A run finished in a few hundred generations: check whether convergence_burn_in and max_generations were set to small fixed numbers. Leave them on auto ; see Why does my run take so long? . Windows warning: verify the release checksum before running the unsigned executable. See SECURITY.md .
